rules.description: Reports a block comment that follows an opening token on its line and ends the line (`if (a) { /* note */`). The tokens are the option `after` (default `{`). A line comment there, and a block comment with code after it on the line, are not reported.

options.description: The tokens a block comment must not follow on their line.
options.name: after

rules.why:
The style keeps a block comment from ending the line of an opening brace. A comment on a line of its own above the first statement says clearly which statement it describes.

To fix, move the comment to its own line.

rules.description: Reports a line comment whose text starts right after the marker (`//text`, `#text`). Not reported: a comment with nothing after the marker, a repeated marker (`////`, `##`), a `--` separator line and a `#!` shebang on the first line. With the option `block` it also checks block comments (`/*a*/`: text right after the opening or before the closing delimiter). The fix inserts the space.

options.description: Check line comments (`// a`). Off, only block comments are checked (with `block`).
options.name: line

options.description: Also check block comments: text right after the opening or before the closing delimiter is reported (`/*a*/`). Exempt: an empty comment, and a delimiter repeated (`/**`, `/***/`). The fix inserts the space.
options.name: block

upstream.note: Line comments only.

rules.why:
One space after the marker is the common way to write comments, and it separates the text from the marker so that the comment reads as text and not as a disabled piece of code. A comment without it is also hard to tell from commented-out code (`//foo();`).

To fix, add the space; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports the body of an `if`, `else`, loop or `when` entry that is one statement without braces (`if (a) b();`, `else c();`, `for (;;) d();`, `while (x) y();`). `else if` is not reported. Style `always` (default) wants braces on every body; style `chain` wants them on the branches of a chain only where one branch has braces, spans lines or passes the line width, and on a loop body that stands on its own line. The language's `curly_style` option overrides the style when the formatter runs the rule. The fix adds the braces.

options.description: `always`: every body; `chain`: see the rule. The `style` row of the language's `curly_style` option overrides it in the formatter.
options.name: style

upstream.note: No option for single-line bodies.

rules.why:
Without braces a second line added later to the body looks as if it belongs to the `if` or loop, but it runs every time. That is how the 2014 Apple `goto fail` bug happened, and braces make the extent of the body visible.

To fix, add the braces; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports a name that a command declares when it does not match the pattern of its class, for languages whose files are a flat list of commands (CMake). The option `names` says which argument of which command is a name and of which class (`command:position:class`), `markers` and `scopes` settle the class of a variable (a marker word among the arguments, or the innermost listed block it is set in), and `patterns` gives each class a regex that the name must match from its start. A class without a pattern is not checked. `reference_start` and `reference_end` cut references such as `${...}` out of a name first, and `ignore_pattern` leaves matching names out.

example.input:
set(lower 1)
set(UPPER 1)
set(lc "" CACHE STRING "x")
set(_OK "" CACHE INTERNAL "x")
set(lc2 "" CACHE STRING INTERNAL)
set(ENV{any} 1)
set(${x} 1)
set(${x}_a 1)
list(LENGTH UPPER out)
foreach(Item a b)
endforeach()
function(F_n Arg)
  set(Local 1)
  set(local 1)
  set(xy 1 PARENT_SCOPE)
endfunction()
macro(m)
  set(xy 1)
  set(XY 1)
endmacro()

options.description: Rows `command:position:class` (`command` may be `command FIRST-ARGUMENT`): the argument at the position (`0`, `-1` for the last, or `1+` for the rest) are names of the class; the class `variable` is told by `markers` and `scopes`.
options.name: names

options.description: Rows `WORD:class`: a command with the argument WORD (or the arguments `WORD WORD`, in a row) declares a variable of the class; the last row that fits wins.
options.name: markers

options.description: Rows `block:class`: a variable set inside the block that starts with the command `block` (the innermost listed one) has the class; the row with no block is the class outside them. An empty class is not checked.
options.name: scopes

options.description: Rows `class:regex`: the regex a name of the class must match from its start.
options.name: patterns

options.description: Where a reference to another name starts inside a name (`${` in CMake); the references, up to the matching `reference_end`, are cut out before the name is matched, and a name that is only references is left out.
options.name: reference_start

options.description: Where a reference ends (`}` in CMake).
options.name: reference_end

options.description: A regex; a name that matches is left out.
options.name: ignore_pattern

rules.why:
A naming convention is only useful when it holds everywhere: with it, a reader can tell from the name what kind of thing it is, and a search finds all of one kind. Without the option rows the rule checks nothing.

To fix, rename the variable or function.

rules.description: Reports a command listed in the option `commands` (for example `function` and `macro` in CMake, compared ignoring case) that has no comment on the line right before it, or whose comment has no text (`#` alone). A comment further up with a blank line between, or code in between, does not count. The option `doc_kinds` limits which comment kinds document (all by default); a comment of another kind counts as an empty one.

example.input:
# Does a thing.
function(a)
endfunction()

# Detached.

function(b)
endfunction()
#
macro(c)
endmacro()
set(d 1)
#[[ block ]]
function(e)
endfunction()
# Text.
#
function(f)
endfunction()

options.description: The commands that need a comment (case ignored).
options.name: commands

options.description: The kinds of comment token that document (none listed: every comment does); a comment of another kind counts as one with no text.
options.name: doc_kinds

rules.why:
A function or macro is called from other files, so a reader meets the name far from its definition. A comment right above it is the place where tools and readers look for what it takes and does.

To fix, write the comment on the line before the definition.

rules.description: Reports a heading written in another style than the document's: `#` before the text (ATX) or the text over a line of `=` or `-` (setext). The option `style` is `atx`, `setext` or `consistent` (the style of the first heading, the default). The fix rewrites a one-line heading of level 1 or 2.

example.fixed:
# Title

  # Section

  ## Sub

## Atx

  Two
  lines
  ---
example.input:
# Title

  Section
  =======

  Sub
  ---

## Atx

  Two
  lines
  ---

options.description: `atx`, `setext`, or `consistent` (the first heading's style).
options.name: style

options.description: The name of the grammar kind of a heading node.
options.name: kind

upstream.note: `consistent` only (the first heading's style); the fix writes a setext heading of one line as atx, the other way is not fixed. No `setext_with_atx` styles.

rules.why:
Two heading styles in one document make it look edited by different hands, and tools that search for headings (outlines, scripts) must know both. Only level 1 and 2 have a setext form, so ATX is the one style that works for every level.

To fix, use the style of the document; the fix does it for level 1 and 2.

rules.description: Reports a key that does not follow one of the allowed naming conventions of the option `allowed` (default `camelCase`; also `PascalCase`, `snake_case`, `kebab-case`, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`). A key with punctuation or white space never matches; `camelCase` also rejects `_` and `-`, and `snake_case` and `kebab-case` reject capitals. Keys that match one of the `ignored_keys` regexes, and a YAML merge key (`<<`), are not checked. There is no fix, because renaming a key changes the data.

example.config:
key-name-casing:
  level: warn
  options:
    allowed: [snake_case, kebab-case]
    ignored_keys: ["^P"]
example.input: {"camelCase": 1, "snake_case": 2, "kebab-case": 3, "PascalCase": 4, "SCREAMING_SNAKE": 5, "a b": 6}

options.description: Accepted conventions: `camelCase`, `PascalCase`, `snake_case`, `kebab-case`, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`. A key is fine when it matches one.
options.name: allowed

options.description: Regular expressions; matching keys stay where they are and are not compared.
options.name: ignored_keys

rules.why:
Configuration and data files are read by programs and people, and one casing for all keys lets both guess a key's name without looking it up. A key in another casing is often a typo or a copy from another file with other conventions.

To fix, rename the key and every place that reads it.

rules.description: Reports a line longer than `max` characters (default 120). With `allow_non_breakable_words` (default on) a line that has no space after its indentation, a leading `#` run or `- ` is not reported (a long URL); `allow_non_breakable_inline_mappings` also allows a YAML `key: value` line whose value has no space.

options.description: Longest allowed line, in characters.
options.name: max

options.description: Do not report a line that has no space after its indentation (and after a leading `#` run or `- `), such as a long URL.
options.name: allow_non_breakable_words

options.description: With `allow_non_breakable_words`, also do not report a `key: value` line whose value has no space. Only in languages that have such lines (YAML).
options.name: allow_non_breakable_inline_mappings

upstream.note: No ignore pattern for `package` and `import` lines.
ktlint_official allows 140 columns (the `max` option defaults to 120); no exemption for package, import and raw-string lines.
No exemptions for code blocks, tables and headings (`code_blocks`, `tables`, `headings`), no `strict`, `stern` or `line_length` per-language defaults.
no allow_non_breakable_words

rules.why:
Long lines do not fit next to each other in a diff or a code review, wrap unpredictably in narrow windows, and hide the end of the line when a view scrolls sideways. The limit is a convention of the project, set with `max`.

To fix, break the line at a natural place.

rules.description: Reports the modifiers of a declaration (`public`, `static`, `final`, `override`, ...) that are not in the order the style of the language wants: for Java the order of the Java Language Specification (`public protected private abstract default static sealed non-sealed final transient volatile synchronized native strictfp`), for Kotlin the order of the Kotlin coding conventions. Annotations and unknown keywords keep their place. The finding sits on the keyword that is out of place, or on the first modifier with the option `report: list`. The fix reorders the keywords.

options.description: Where a finding is reported: on the keyword that is out of place, or on the first token of the modifier list.
options.name: report

upstream.note: Annotations are not checked against the modifiers.
The shared rule over the `#modifiers` node; ktlint's order, annotations stay in place

rules.why:
Modifiers in a fixed order are easier to scan: the access level is always first, so a reader and a search for `public static` find every declaration alike. The order carries no meaning for the compiler, so no behaviour changes.

To fix, reorder the modifiers; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports a key that a mapping has twice, after decoding escapes and quotes (`{"a": 1, "\u0061": 2}` has `a` twice). It reads the mappings of the language's grammar: JSON and JSONC objects, YAML and TOML mappings, JavaScript object literals, and similar entries of other languages. A YAML merge key (`<<`) may repeat, and the option `merge_keys: forbid` reports a second one too. The second key is reported, the first is shown as related.

options.description: Languages with a merge key (YAML `<<`) only. `allow` skips merge keys, which may repeat; `forbid` reports a second one like any other duplicate key.
options.name: merge_keys

upstream.note: partial
repeated `v-on` handlers and slots are allowed, and `class` next to `:class` is not a repeat

rules.why:
Parsers disagree on what a duplicate means: many keep the last value, some the first, some reject the file. The value that is lost is silent, so a file can mean something different in two tools, and the second entry is often a copy that was meant to have another name.

To fix, remove one of the keys, or give it its own name.

rules.description: Reports a section that has the same name as an earlier section of the file (INI and EditorConfig: the section header, for EditorConfig the glob).

example.input:
[*.cs]
indent_size = 4

[*.vb]
indent_size = 2

[*.cs]
tab_width = 4
[*.CS]
tab_width = 4

rules.why:
Readers of the format handle repeated sections in different ways: some merge them, some keep only the last, so the settings of one of them may be lost or applied in an order that is hard to see.

To fix, merge the two sections into one.

rules.description: Reports a comment with no text. An empty block comment (`/**/`) is reported wherever it is. An empty line comment is reported only when it begins or ends a run of comment lines, because a bare `//` between two comment lines separates paragraphs; the option `separators` reports those too.

options.description: Also report an empty line comment between two comments.
options.name: separators

rules.why:
An empty comment says nothing: it is a leftover of a deleted comment or of an unfinished one, and a reader stops to look for the meaning that is not there.

To fix, write the text or delete the comment.

rules.description: Reports a key that is empty or only white space after decoding escapes (`"": 4`).
rules.why:
A property with no name cannot be reached the usual ways: a dotted path, a command line option or an environment variable has no spelling for it, and some consumers fail on it. It is nearly always a missing name.

To fix, give the key a name.

rules.description: Reports a tab character in a line; a run of tabs is one report. The option `ignore_kinds` lists token kinds whose tabs are not reported (for example the code of a Markdown fence), and `indentation_only` reports only the tabs in the white space that starts a line.

example.input:
if(A)
  	set(x 1)
  set(y	2)
endif()

options.description: Kinds of tokens whose tabs are not reported (for example the code of a fence).
options.name: ignore_kinds

options.description: Report only the tabs in the whitespace that starts a line.
options.name: indentation_only

upstream.note: Reported on the tab run, as markdownlint does; no `spaces_per_tab` fix, no `ignore_code_languages`; `code_blocks` off is the option `ignore_kinds` naming the code tokens.

rules.why:
A tab is as wide as each reader's editor and tool makes it, so text that is aligned with tabs looks different in a diff, in a review and on the web. Spaces look the same everywhere. Some formats (YAML indentation) do not accept tabs at all.

To fix, replace the tab with spaces.

rules.description: Reports a block comment that fits on one line and ends its line (`/* text */`): it is written as a line comment. Documentation comments (`/**`), empty comments, comments with code after them on the same line and languages without a line comment marker are not reported. The fix turns it into a line comment.
rules.why:
A line comment is the plain form for a short note. A block comment on one line is usually left over from a longer comment, and the next edit adds a second line inside it.

To fix, use `// text`; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports spaces or tabs at the end of a line, from the first one to the line break. Every language is checked the same way, so Markdown's two-space line break is reported too.

example.input:
text

fine

upstream.note: also reported inside pre and raw text
Also reports inside block scalars, where the content is data and the formatter keeps it.

rules.why:
Trailing white space cannot be seen, adds nothing, and many editors strip it, so a later edit shows a change on a line the author did not touch and makes diffs and blame noisy.

To fix, delete it.

rules.description: Removes a return type that the language gives every function with a block body anyway (`fun f(): Unit { }` in Kotlin; the types come from the option `redundant_return_types`). The functions are those with a block body, the type is the one after the colon that follows the parameters. The rule works in the formatter, which applies it when it is on (Kotlin has it on); `sudsy lint` makes no report for it.
rules.why:
The type says nothing the reader does not already know, and it makes the signature longer. `Unit` is what a block body returns when it has no `return` of a value.

To fix, delete the colon and the type; the formatter does it.

rules.description: Reports the items of a sequence that are not in order, for sequences of only strings or only numbers (ascending by default; numbers compare as numbers). A sequence of other or mixed items is skipped. The fewest items that would have to move are reported, and the first report carries the fix. The fix is unsafe: the order of a sequence can be data. Options: `direction`, `compare` (`ordinal`, `case_insensitive`, `natural`), `min_values` (default 2), `blank_line_groups` and `path_patterns` (only the sequences whose key path matches one).

example.config:
sorted-array-values:
  level: warn
  options:
    direction: desc

options.description: `asc` or `desc`.
options.name: direction

options.description: `ordinal` (code points), `case_insensitive`, or `natural` (digit runs compare as numbers: `a2` before `a10`).
options.name: compare

options.description: Sequences with fewer items are not checked.
options.name: min_values

options.description: Sort each run of entries between blank lines on its own.
options.name: blank_line_groups

options.description: Regular expressions; only mappings (sequences) whose key path matches one are checked. The path is `a.b[0].c` (`["odd key"]` for keys that are not identifiers), empty for the root; none listed means everywhere. A TOML table counts as its header key and an array table is not indexed.
options.name: path_patterns

upstream.note: one ordering per rule configuration (ESLint takes a list of {pathPattern, order} entries with different orders per path; use `overrides` per file instead); no `key` (sort objects by a property), no explicit value lists or `valuePattern`, mixed or non-scalar arrays are skipped, report positions when several equally short moves exist
Taplo sorts only values not separated by blank lines; the rule sorts the whole array.

rules.why:
A list that is kept sorted is easy to scan and to merge: new entries go to one place, and two branches that add different entries rarely conflict. The rule only makes sense where the order is not data, so it is off by default.

To fix, sort the items, or turn the rule off for that list with `path_patterns`.

rules.description: Reports the keys of a mapping that are not in order (alphabetical by default). By default the fewest keys that would have to move are reported (`report: moved`), `misplaced` reports every key that sorts before one above it. The first report carries the fix. Comments on lines of their own stay where they are and a comment after an entry moves with it. Options: `order` (keys that come first), `direction`, `compare` (`ordinal`, `case_insensitive`, `natural`), `ignored_keys`, `min_keys` (default 2), `blank_line_groups`, `path_patterns` and `has_properties` (only mappings that have all of these keys). The fix is unsafe: moving a YAML anchor below its alias breaks the document.

example.config:
sorted-keys:
  level: warn
  options:
    blank_line_groups: true

options.description: Keys that come first, in this order; the rest follow in the configured order.
options.name: order

options.description: `asc` or `desc`.
options.name: direction

options.description: `ordinal` (code points), `case_insensitive`, or `natural` (digit runs compare as numbers: `a2` before `a10`).
options.name: compare

options.description: Regular expressions; matching keys stay where they are and are not compared.
options.name: ignored_keys

options.description: Mappings with fewer keys are not checked.
options.name: min_keys

options.description: Sort each run of entries between blank lines on its own.
options.name: blank_line_groups

options.description: Regular expressions; only mappings (sequences) whose key path matches one are checked. The path is `a.b[0].c` (`["odd key"]` for keys that are not identifiers), empty for the root; none listed means everywhere. A TOML table counts as its header key and an array table is not indexed.
options.name: path_patterns

options.description: Only mappings that have all of these keys are checked.
options.name: has_properties

options.description: Which keys are reported. `moved`: the fewest keys that would have to move (eslint-plugin-jsonc). `misplaced`: every key that sorts before one above it (yamllint).
options.name: report

upstream.note: no groupByNesting; natural order is not guaranteed identical to Biome's for non-ASCII keys (unverified)

one ordering per rule configuration (ESLint's list of entries with different orders per path: use `overrides` per file); no per-key `keyPattern` orders and no `ignore` order type (`ignored_keys` is the closest); report positions when several equally short moves exist
Upstream picks the kinds to sort (fields, values, selections, variables, arguments, definitions) and a `groups` order; sorted-keys has no per-kind switch and does not sort definitions.
Taplo sorts only keys not separated by blank lines; the rule sorts the whole table.
A lint rule, not a formatter option.
no locale collation: yamllint's global `locale` uses the C library's collation; Sudsy offers `compare: ordinal | case_insensitive | natural` instead

rules.why:
Keys in a fixed order are quick to look up, and two branches that add different keys to a sorted file rarely conflict. The order of a mapping is usually not data, but where a tool reads it (a build order, a dependency list that is applied top down) the rule should be limited with `path_patterns` or turned off.

To fix, sort the keys; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports more than `max` blank lines (default 1) right before a top-level statement (a direct child of the file that starts its line). The first statement of a file may have one more. Block arms and closers of the language (`else`, `endif`) are not checked. A line with only white space counts as blank. The finding is on the first token of the statement.

options.description: The longest run of blank lines allowed before a statement.
options.name: max

rules.why:
A run of blank lines is a visual gap that separates parts of a file. One blank line separates statements well, and more leave holes that make the file look as if something is missing.

To fix, delete the extra blank lines.

rules.description: Reports a statement, the closing parenthesis of a multi-line statement or a comment between statements that is not at the column that its block depth gives (depth times `size`, default 2) in a language whose files are a flat list of commands with block words such as `if` and `endif` (CMake). With `allow_unindented` a token in column 0 is accepted at any depth. A comment between statements may sit at the depth of the statement before or after it. The fix rewrites the white space before the token.

options.description: Columns per block depth.
options.name: size

options.description: Accept a token at column 0 whatever its depth.
options.name: allow_unindented

rules.why:
In a flat list of commands the indentation is the only sign of the blocks, because nothing but the block words delimit them. When it is wrong the reader sees a different nesting than the one that runs.

To fix, indent to the block depth; the fix does it.

rules.description: Reports a comment that disables rules of another tool (`# rubocop:disable Foo/Bar`) by a `Group/Name` whose group the tool does not have, for example the group of an extension that is not installed. A name inside a known group is not checked (the groups are listed in the grammar's `suppress directive-group` rows).

example.input:
x = :true
y = :ok
z = 'a #{b}'
"a #{1} #{x} #{[:a]}"
/(?<a>x)(y)/
/(?<a>x)(?:y)/
a = a
@b ||= @b
c = d
f == 0.1
f == 0
begin
  x
end while y
case x
when 1
when 2 then z
end
begin
  1
rescue Exception
end
begin
  1
rescue
end
# rubocop:disable Foo/Bar
h = { true: 1 }

upstream.note: only the unknown department of a cop name; not the other malformed directives or an unknown cop of a known department

rules.why:
A directive with a group the tool does not have does not suppress what the author expects, so the finding stays or the directive is ignored. It is usually a typo in the group name or an extension that is missing in the project.

To fix, correct the name, or install the extension.

rules.description: A number that a double-precision parser (JavaScript, most JSON libraries) cannot hold: an integer beyond 2^53 - 1, a value that overflows to infinity, underflows to zero or is subnormal.

upstream.note: lone UTF-16 surrogates in strings are not reported

rules.description: The alpha value of `rgb()`, `hsl()`, `hwb()`, `lab()`, `lch()`, `oklab()`, `oklch()` or `color()` written as a number (`/ 0.5` is `/ 50%`); the comma form of `rgba()` and `hsla()` counts too.
An `@extend` of anything but a placeholder selector; a selector with interpolation is left alone.
A `@function` whose name does not match the `pattern` option (a regex). An empty pattern allows everything.

options.description: The regex a function name must match.
options.name: pattern

rules.description: An `@if` that compares with `null` (`== null`, `!= null`): write `not $a` or `$a`.
An `@include` of a mixin with empty parentheses (`@include foo()`); a `using (...)` clause after them is left alone.
A `@mixin` whose name does not match the `pattern` option (a regex). An empty pattern allows everything.

options.description: The regex a mixin name must match.
options.name: pattern

rules.description: An at-rule (vendor prefix left out) that is not in the `list` option. An empty list allows everything.

options.description: The allowed at-rules, without `@`: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.description: The condition of `@if`, `@else if` and `@while` written in parentheses (`@if ($a == 1)`).
An at-rule (vendor prefix left out) that is in the `list` option.

options.description: The disallowed at-rules, without `@`: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: list

rules.description: An at-rule needs a blank line before it, unless a comment is right before it; the first at-rule of a block, and a blockless one right after a blockless one of the same name (`@import` lines), take none.
A deprecated at-rule (`@document`, `@nest`, `@viewport`).

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.description: An at-rule that no CSS specification lists. Vendor-prefixed ones are left out; SCSS has its own (`@include`, `@mixin`, ...), and Less at-rules are not checked. Tailwind's are left out by default.

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

upstream.note: Less at-rules are not told apart (detached ruleset calls look like at-rules), so none is reported in Less.
Less at-rules are not told apart (detached ruleset calls look like at-rules), so none is reported in Less.

rules.description: A vendor-prefixed at-rule that autoprefixer knows the standard one of.

options.description: Names left out: names, or `/regex/`.
options.name: ignore

rules.description: A rule or at-rule block with nothing in it, comments included.
`rgba()` and `hsla()`, the legacy names of `rgb()` and `hsl()`.
`rgb()`, `rgba()`, `hsl()` or `hsla()` with the legacy comma-separated arguments (`rgb(0, 0, 0)` is `rgb(0 0 0)`), also with a call such as `var()` as an argument.
A hex color that can be written with three or four digits (`#aabbcc` is `#abc`); with the `style` option set to `long`, one that is written short.

options.description: `short` reports colors that can be shortened, `long` those that are short.
options.name: style

rules.description: A hex color: write a named color or a function instead.
A hex color that does not have 3, 4, 6 or 8 hex digits.
A `/* */` comment on a line of its own needs a blank line before it, unless it comes first in a block, shares a line with code or is a `stylelint-` directive; a `//` comment is another rule's.

upstream.note: `//` comments are left to double-slash-comment-empty-line-before, as stylelint ignores them

rules.description: A `@container` name that does not match the `pattern` option (a regex). An empty pattern allows everything.

options.description: The regex a container name must match.

rules.description: Reports an equality or inequality with a boolean literal on either side (`x == true`, `x !== false`, `true == x`, `x != False`). The option `literals` lists the texts that count as boolean literals, `not_operators` the operators that are not a comparison of value (Python `is`). Off by default.

x != False
True == x

upstream.note: Only a comparison with a boolean literal, not the double negation or the conditional forms.

rules.why:
Comparing a condition with `true` or `false` adds a token pair that says what the expression already says. `x == true` reads longer than `x`, and for values that are not strictly boolean (a number, a string) the comparison also means something other than the plain test.

To fix, use the expression itself, or `!` before it.

rules.description: Reports an assignment used as the condition of an `if`, a ternary or a loop (`if (a = b)`, `while (x = next())`) when it is not wrapped in parentheses of its own (`if ((a = b))` is accepted). Python's `:=` is left alone. Off by default.

upstream.note: only the default `except-parens` mode
`a && b = c` is the Ruby rule no-assignment-in-logical-condition; over several lines is reported at the first line of the condition, RuboCop reports the assignment line

rules.why:
An assignment in a condition is nearly always a typing error for `==`: the test then stores a value and branches on it, and the comparison the author meant never happens. A reader cannot tell the two intentions apart.

To fix, write `==` if a comparison was meant, or move the assignment out of the condition (or add the extra parentheses) if it was meant.

rules.description: Reports an equality or a comparison whose two sides are both literals (`1 === 2`, `"a" < "b"`). An operand that is an expression of literals (`1 + 1 === 2`) is not reported.

upstream.note: only two literals compared

rules.why:
The result of a comparison of two literals is fixed when the code is written, so one branch of the `if` never runs. It is usually a leftover of debugging, or of a value that was meant to be a variable.

To fix, compare the variable, or replace the test with its result.

rules.description: Reports the condition of an `if`, a ternary or a loop that is a literal (`if (true)`, `if (0)`, `x = true ? 1 : 2`, `while (false)`). The usual forms of an endless loop (`while (true)`, `while (1)`, `for (;true;)`, `do {} while (true)`) are left alone.

upstream.note: literals only (no object, function or `!` forms)

rules.why:
With a literal as the test one branch always runs and the other never does, so the test is either dead code or a switch that was left on while debugging.

To fix, remove the test and keep the branch that runs, or put the real condition in.

rules.description: Reports an arm of a `switch`, `match`, `when` or `case` whose test is the same as the test of an earlier arm of the same statement (`case 1:` twice). The second arm is reported, the first is shown as related.
rules.why:
Only the first arm with that test can run, so the second is dead code. It is usually a copy that should have had another value, and the case it was meant for is then unhandled.

To fix, change the test to the value it was meant for, or merge the two arms.

rules.description: Reports a block with no statement and no comment as the body of an `if`, `else`, loop, `try` or `finally` (`if (a) { }`, `for (;;) { }`). A comment inside counts as content. A bare `{ }` and a function body are not reported, and an empty `catch` is the rule `no-empty-catch`. With `comment_handles` off a comment does not count. With `waiting_loops` an empty loop whose condition is a call is a wait and is left alone, and so is a loop whose head matches `ignored_loop_heads`.

options.name: comment_handles

options.description: Leave alone an empty loop whose condition is a call
options.name: waiting_loops

a bare `{}` block statement and an empty `switch` body are not read

rules.why:
An empty block is usually a branch that was started and never filled in, or code that was deleted around it. The reader cannot tell whether the nothing is meant.

To fix, write the code, or say in a comment that nothing is intended.

rules.description: Reports a `catch`, `except` or `rescue` clause whose body has no statement and no comment (`catch (e) { }`; in Python a lone `pass` counts as no statement). With the option `comment_handles` off a comment does not count either. With `broad_only` only a clause that catches everything, or one of the exception types of the option `types`, is reported.

options.name: types

rules.why:
An empty handler swallows the error without a trace: the program goes on in a state it did not expect, and the failure shows up later far from its cause, with nothing in the logs.

To fix, handle the error, log it, or let it propagate; if ignoring it is right, say why in a comment.

rules.description: Reports an assignment whose two sides are the same tokens (`x = x`, `x.y = x.y`, `x[0] = x[0]`, `x ||= x`). The option `operators` lists the operators that store the right side as it is (`=`, `||=`, `&&=`, `??=`); `x += x` is not reported.

options.description: The assignment operators that store the right side as it is
options.name: operators

upstream.note: the `props` option is always on; only identifiers and static member chains are compared
not multiple assignment (`a, b = a, b`)

rules.why:
The assignment changes nothing, or only calls a getter and a setter for nothing. It is nearly always a typing error where the right side should have been another variable, such as a parameter with the same name as a field.

To fix, name the right variable, or delete the statement.

rules.description: Reports an equality or comparison whose two sides are the same tokens (`x === x`, `x < x`). `x != x` used as a test for NaN is reported too. Two calls (`f() === f()`) count as the same tokens and are reported.
rules.why:
For a value the result is the same every time (except for NaN), so the test is dead or a typing error: the author compared a variable with itself instead of with another one.

To fix, compare with the right value; to test for NaN, use `isNaN` or the language's own check.

rules.description: Reports a statement that can never run: after `return`, `throw`, `break` or `continue`, after an `if`/`else` or `try` that always jumps, or after a loop that never ends. Only the first statement of such a run is reported. Where the language has a flow layer (C#) it also covers constant conditions and calls that do not return (`does_not_return` in `semantics:`, the option `non_returning_calls`). Hoisted declarations and empty statements are left out. Removing the statement is offered as an editor quick fix only, because unreachable code usually signals a bug.

options.description: With a flow layer, treat the code after a call that never returns (`[DoesNotReturn]`, `does_not_return` in `semantics:`) as unreachable. A compiler does not, so turn this off to report exactly what it reports.
options.name: non_returning_calls

upstream.note: the code after `panic`, `os.Exit`, `log.Fatal*` and `t.Fatal*` is not read as unreachable

rules.why:
Code that cannot run is either a leftover or a sign that an earlier `return` or `throw` is in the wrong place, in which case what the author expected to run does not.

To fix, delete the statement, or move the jump that makes it unreachable.

rules.description: Reports an `apk add` without the `--no-cache` flag. A `RUN` with a `--mount` of type `cache` or `tmpfs` on `/var/cache/apk` is not reported, since nothing is stored in the image there.

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN apk add curl
RUN apk add --no-cache curl=8.5.0-r0
RUN apk add --no-cache --virtual .deps gcc=13.2.1-r0 musl-dev=1.2.4-r2
RUN apk add --no-cache ./pkg.apk
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apk apk add curl=8

rules.why:
Without `--no-cache`, `apk add` keeps the downloaded package index in `/var/cache/apk`. That copy is written into the layer and stays in the image, making it larger for data nobody reads at run time.

`--no-cache` fetches the index for this one command and stores nothing; it replaces the older pair `apk update` and `rm -rf /var/cache/apk/*`.

rules.description:
Reports an `apk add` that names a package without a version. A package is pinned when its name has `=`, `~`, `<` or `>` (`curl=8.5.0-r0`, `curl~8.5`) or when it is a local `.apk` file; a variable such as `$PKGS` counts as unpinned, because its content is unknown.

The values of options that take one (`--virtual NAME`, `-t NAME`, `--repository URL`, `-X URL`) are not taken for packages, and an `apk add` with no package is fine.

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN apk add curl
RUN apk add --no-cache curl=8.5.0-r0
RUN apk add --no-cache --virtual .deps gcc=13.2.1-r0 musl-dev=1.2.4-r2
RUN apk add --no-cache ./pkg.apk
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apk apk add curl=8

rules.why:
Without a version, `apk add` installs whatever the Alpine repository holds on the day of the build. Rebuilding the same Dockerfile later can give an image with other package versions, and a new release that breaks your program arrives without any change on your side.

A pinned build is repeatable. The price is upkeep: when the repository replaces a version with a newer one, the build fails until you update the pin.

rules.description: Reports an `apt-get install` that also installs recommended packages. `--no-install-recommends` (or `-o APT::Install-Recommends=false`) stops that. Other `apt-get` commands are not checked.

example.input:
FROM debian:12
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install curl
RUN apt-get install -y curl=7.88 wget=1.21
RUN apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl
RUN apt-get install -qq -y -t stable curl=7.88
RUN apt-get -y install foo/stable
RUN apt-get install -yq ./a.deb
RUN apt-get install --yes \
    curl \
    git
RUN apt-get update

# a blank line or a comment before an instruction does not hide it
RUN apt-get install -y curl=7.88

rules.why:
By default `apt-get` also installs the packages that a package only recommends, which it does not need to run. In an image they add size and build time, and more software to patch and to be attacked through.

With the flag only the real dependencies are installed; name anything else you need yourself.

rules.description: Reports an `apt-get install` of a package without a version. A package is pinned when its name has `=` (`curl=7.88.1-10`) or `/` (`curl/stable`, a release), or when it is a `.deb` file. The value of `-t` or `--target-release` is not taken for a package. A variable such as `$PKGS` counts as unpinned.

example.input:
FROM debian:12
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install curl
RUN apt-get install -y curl=7.88 wget=1.21
RUN apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl
RUN apt-get install -qq -y -t stable curl=7.88
RUN apt-get -y install foo/stable
RUN apt-get install -yq ./a.deb
RUN apt-get install --yes \
    curl \
    git
RUN apt-get update

# a blank line or a comment before an instruction does not hide it
RUN apt-get install -y curl=7.88

rules.why:
An unpinned install takes the newest version the distribution offers on the day of the build. Two builds of one Dockerfile can then differ, and a new release can break the image without any change in your code.

Pinned versions make the build repeatable. Debian and Ubuntu remove old versions from their repositories, so a pin stops resolving after a while and needs updating.

rules.description: Reports an `apt-get install` that does not answer apt's prompts. The flags that do are `-y`, `--yes`, `--assume-yes` and `-qq` (also `-q=2` and `--quiet` twice), which implies yes; they may stand anywhere in the command (`apt-get -y install` is fine). Other `apt-get` commands are not checked.

example.input:
FROM debian:12
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install curl
RUN apt-get install -y curl=7.88 wget=1.21
RUN apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl
RUN apt-get install -qq -y -t stable curl=7.88
RUN apt-get -y install foo/stable
RUN apt-get install -yq ./a.deb
RUN apt-get install --yes \
    curl \
    git
RUN apt-get update

# a blank line or a comment before an instruction does not hide it
RUN apt-get install -y curl=7.88

rules.why: A build has no terminal to answer questions. When `apt-get` needs a confirmation, for example because the install pulls in additional packages, it prints `Do you want to continue? [Y/n] Abort.` and exits with an error, which fails the `RUN` and the build.

rules.description: Reports a `COPY --from` that names its own stage. That is `COPY --from=build` in the stage that `FROM alpine AS build` starts. Names are compared without regard to case.

example.input:
FROM alpine
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM build
FROM scratch
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM $BASE
FROM alpine:3 AS Build
FROM BUILD
FROM localhost:5000/img
FROM localhost:5000/img:1
FROM alpine@sha256:abc
USER root
USER app
USER 0:0
COPY --from=build /a /b
COPY --from=nope /a /b
COPY --from=BUILD /a /b
COPY --from=0 /a /b
COPY --from=99 /a /b
COPY --from=alpine:3 /a /b
CMD ["a"]
CMD ["b"]
ENTRYPOINT ["a"]
ENTRYPOINT ["b"]
HEALTHCHECK CMD a
HEALTHCHECK CMD b
FROM alpine:3 AS last
COPY --from=LAST /a /b
USER app
CMD ["a"]
USER root

rules.why: A stage cannot copy from itself: its content does not exist yet while it is built, and BuildKit stops with a circular dependency error. The source is usually an earlier stage, or the build context (then drop `--from`).

rules.description: Reports a `COPY --from=name` that names no stage defined earlier. Not reported: the number of an earlier stage (`--from=0`) and an image reference with a `:` (`--from=nginx:1`). A stage defined further down does not count. Names are compared without regard to case.

example.input:
FROM alpine
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM build
FROM scratch
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM $BASE
FROM alpine:3 AS Build
FROM BUILD
FROM localhost:5000/img
FROM localhost:5000/img:1
FROM alpine@sha256:abc
USER root
USER app
USER 0:0
COPY --from=build /a /b
COPY --from=nope /a /b
COPY --from=BUILD /a /b
COPY --from=0 /a /b
COPY --from=99 /a /b
COPY --from=alpine:3 /a /b
CMD ["a"]
CMD ["b"]
ENTRYPOINT ["a"]
ENTRYPOINT ["b"]
HEALTHCHECK CMD a
HEALTHCHECK CMD b
FROM alpine:3 AS last
COPY --from=LAST /a /b
USER app
CMD ["a"]
USER root

rules.why: Docker does not fail on an unknown name: it takes it for an image and pulls it from the registry. A typo in a stage name (`buidler`) or a reference to a stage defined further down copies files from whatever image has that name, or fails only when the pull fails.

rules.description: Reports an `ADD` that only copies. That is an `ADD` with no URL (`http://`, `https://`) and no archive (a name ending in `.tar`, `.gz`, `.tgz`, `.xz`, `.bz2` and the like) among its arguments.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch
FROM alpine:3@sha256:abc
WORKDIR app
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443
CMD node server.js
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
ENTRYPOINT /run.sh
ONBUILD CMD echo hi
ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN x
ONBUILD MAINTAINER x
MAINTAINER a@b.c
COPY --from=0 / /
COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/
COPY a /dest
ADD app.js /app/
ADD app.tar.gz /app/
ADD https://example.com/f /app/
USER app
USER 1000:1000
USER $UID
ENV DB_PASSWORD=x
ENV A=1 NPM_TOKEN=y
ARG GITHUB_TOKEN
ARG VERSION=1
ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=x

upstream.note: Reports an ADD with no URL and no archive among its arguments; hadolint reports one source that is neither.

rules.why:
`ADD` does more than copy: it unpacks local tar archives and downloads URLs. For a plain file or folder that is a surprise, since an archive you meant to copy is extracted and a value that turns out to be a URL starts a download. `COPY` only copies, so the instruction says what happens.

Keep `ADD` for unpacking an archive into the image.

rules.description: Reports a `COPY` with several sources whose destination does not end with `/` (`COPY a b /app`). The JSON form, a single source and a heredoc (`<<`) are not checked.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch
FROM alpine:3@sha256:abc
WORKDIR app
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443
CMD node server.js
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
ENTRYPOINT /run.sh
ONBUILD CMD echo hi
ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN x
ONBUILD MAINTAINER x
MAINTAINER a@b.c
COPY --from=0 / /
COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/
COPY a /dest
ADD app.js /app/
ADD app.tar.gz /app/
ADD https://example.com/f /app/
USER app
USER 1000:1000
USER $UID
ENV DB_PASSWORD=x
ENV A=1 NPM_TOKEN=y
ARG GITHUB_TOKEN
ARG VERSION=1
ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=x

upstream.note: The shell form only; the JSON form is not checked.

rules.why: With several sources the destination must be a directory, and Docker takes a destination without a trailing slash for a file name. The build stops with an error that the destination of a copy of several sources must end with `/`.

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that updates the apt package lists and does not delete them. It runs `apt-get update` or `apt update` and has no `rm` of `/var/lib/apt/lists` after it in the same `RUN`. `apt-get clean` does not count, it empties another directory. A `RUN` with a `--mount` of type `cache` or `tmpfs` on `/var/lib/apt/lists` is not reported.

example.input:
FROM debian:12
RUN a
RUN b
# a comment between does not matter
RUN c
ENV A=1
RUN d
RUN e && f
RUN g
RUN h $(i)
RUN j
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/x k
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/x l
RUN m
RUN ["n", "o"]
RUN ["p"]

RUN a | b
RUN a || b
RUN ["a", "b"]
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]
RUN a | b
FROM debian:12
RUN a | b
RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y a
RUN apt update
RUN apt-get update && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y a && rm -fr "/var/lib/apt/lists"
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt/lists apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y a

upstream.note: Only the RUN that runs `apt-get update` is checked, and any `rm` of a path under /var/lib/apt/lists in it counts, as hadolint does.

rules.why:
`apt-get update` downloads the package index files into `/var/lib/apt/lists`, often tens of megabytes that no program needs at run time. They are written into the layer of that `RUN`, and deleting them in a later `RUN` hides them but does not make the image smaller, because the earlier layer still holds the files.

To fix, remove them in the same `RUN`: `apt-get update && apt-get install -y ... && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`.

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that installs with dnf and does not clean the cache. It runs `dnf install`, `upgrade` or `reinstall` (also `microdnf`, and the short forms `in`, `up`, `rei`) and has no `dnf clean all` or `microdnf clean all` after it in the same `RUN`. An `rm -rf /var/cache/libdnf5*` written exactly so is accepted as well.

example.input:
FROM fedora:40
RUN yum install curl
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && yum clean all
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && rm -rf /var/cache/yum/*
RUN yum install -y nginx-1.2 && yum clean all
RUN dnf install curl
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0 && dnf clean all
RUN microdnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y ./a.rpm && dnf clean all
RUN zypper install curl
RUN zypper install -y curl=7.0 && zypper clean
RUN zypper install -y curl
RUN zypper dist-upgrade
RUN zypper -n in curl=1 && zypper cc

rules.why:
`dnf` stores the metadata and packages it downloaded under `/var/cache`. That cache is written into the layer and stays in the image, adding size that nothing uses at run time.

Clean it in the same `RUN`: a later `RUN` cannot shrink a layer that was already written.

rules.description: Reports a `dnf install`, `dnf groupinstall` or `dnf localinstall` (also with `microdnf`) without `-y` or `--assumeyes`.

example.input:
FROM fedora:40
RUN yum install curl
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && yum clean all
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && rm -rf /var/cache/yum/*
RUN yum install -y nginx-1.2 && yum clean all
RUN dnf install curl
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0 && dnf clean all
RUN microdnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y ./a.rpm && dnf clean all
RUN zypper install curl
RUN zypper install -y curl=7.0 && zypper clean
RUN zypper install -y curl
RUN zypper dist-upgrade
RUN zypper -n in curl=1 && zypper cc

rules.why: Before it installs, dnf asks `Is this ok [y/N]`. A build has no terminal to answer, so dnf aborts with `Operation aborted` and the `RUN` fails.

rules.description: Reports a stage name that an earlier stage already uses, as in `FROM a AS app` followed by `FROM b AS app`. Names are compared without regard to case, as Docker does.

example.input:
FROM alpine
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM build
FROM scratch
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM $BASE
FROM alpine:3 AS Build
FROM BUILD
FROM localhost:5000/img
FROM localhost:5000/img:1
FROM alpine@sha256:abc
USER root
USER app
USER 0:0
COPY --from=build /a /b
COPY --from=nope /a /b
COPY --from=BUILD /a /b
COPY --from=0 /a /b
COPY --from=99 /a /b
COPY --from=alpine:3 /a /b
CMD ["a"]
CMD ["b"]
ENTRYPOINT ["a"]
ENTRYPOINT ["b"]
HEALTHCHECK CMD a
HEALTHCHECK CMD b
FROM alpine:3 AS last
COPY --from=LAST /a /b
USER app
CMD ["a"]
USER root

rules.why: `FROM name` and `COPY --from=name` refer to a stage by its name. With two stages of one name the builder cannot tell which one is meant, so Docker rejects the file.

rules.description: Reports an `EXPOSE` with a port number above 65535. Several ports, `/tcp` and `/udp` suffixes and ranges (`8000-70000`) are all checked; a variable is not.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch
FROM alpine:3@sha256:abc
WORKDIR app
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443
CMD node server.js
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
ENTRYPOINT /run.sh
ONBUILD CMD echo hi
ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN x
ONBUILD MAINTAINER x
MAINTAINER a@b.c
COPY --from=0 / /
COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/
COPY a /dest
ADD app.js /app/
ADD app.tar.gz /app/
ADD https://example.com/f /app/
USER app
USER 1000:1000
USER $UID
ENV DB_PASSWORD=x
ENV A=1 NPM_TOKEN=y
ARG GITHUB_TOKEN
ARG VERSION=1
ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=x

rules.why: TCP and UDP ports are 16-bit numbers from 0 to 65535. A larger number is a typo (a digit too many), and Docker rejects it as an invalid port, so the build fails.

rules.description: Reports an instruction other than `ARG` before the first `FROM`. Comments, parser directives and blank lines are allowed there.

example.input:
ARG V=1
RUN echo hi
FROM alpine:3
RUN echo ok

rules.why: Every instruction works on a build stage, and a stage starts with `FROM`. Only `ARG` may come first, because its value can be used in the `FROM` line (`ARG VERSION=3` then `FROM alpine:${VERSION}`). Any other instruction first makes the Dockerfile invalid, and Docker rejects it.

rules.description: Reports a `gem install` (or `gem i`) of a gem without a version: `rails` instead of `rails:7.1.3`. `-v` or `--version` pins as well. The values of options that take one (`--source URL`, `-i DIR`, `--platform NAME`) are not taken for gems.

example.input:
FROM node:20
RUN pip install flask
RUN pip install flask==2.0 "requests>=2"
RUN pip3 install -r requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -i https://x/simple flask==1
RUN pip install .
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b@v1
RUN npm install
RUN npm install express
RUN npm install express@4 @scope/pkg@1
RUN npm install --loglevel verbose express@4
RUN npm install ./local
RUN npm i express
RUN npm add express@4
RUN gem install rails
RUN gem install --no-document rails
RUN gem install --source https://rubygems.org rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails -v 7.0
RUN go install example.com/x
RUN go install example.com/x@v1
RUN go install example.com/x@latest

upstream.note: hadolint drops the word after every flag; Sudsy does the same (`skip-flag-args: *`), so cases it parses differently with options can differ.

rules.why: Without a version `gem install` takes the newest release on the day of the build, and so a major release of a gem can break the image, and two builds of one Dockerfile give different results.

rules.description: Reports a `go install` or `go get` of a package without a version, or at `latest` or `none` (`example.com/tool@latest`). `example.com/tool@v1.4.0` is pinned. A path that starts with `.` or `/` (a package of the current module) is not reported.

example.input:
FROM node:20
RUN pip install flask
RUN pip install flask==2.0 "requests>=2"
RUN pip3 install -r requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -i https://x/simple flask==1
RUN pip install .
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b@v1
RUN npm install
RUN npm install express
RUN npm install express@4 @scope/pkg@1
RUN npm install --loglevel verbose express@4
RUN npm install ./local
RUN npm i express
RUN npm add express@4
RUN gem install rails
RUN gem install --no-document rails
RUN gem install --source https://rubygems.org rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails -v 7.0
RUN go install example.com/x
RUN go install example.com/x@v1
RUN go install example.com/x@latest

upstream.note: `go install` and `go get`; `go run` is not checked.

rules.why:
`@latest` builds whatever release is newest on the day of the build, so the tool in the image changes between builds and a new release can fail or behave differently. Without any version, `go install` uses the version in the `go.mod` of the working directory (and fails when there is none), and `go get` moves it to the latest release. In both cases the Dockerfile does not say which version ends up in the image.

Write the version: `go install example.com/tool@v1.4.0`.

rules.description: Reports a `CMD`, `ENTRYPOINT` or `HEALTHCHECK CMD` in shell form. That is `CMD node server.js` instead of the JSON array form `CMD ["node", "server.js"]`. The same instruction after `ONBUILD` is not reported.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch
FROM alpine:3@sha256:abc
WORKDIR app
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443
CMD node server.js
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
ENTRYPOINT /run.sh
ONBUILD CMD echo hi
ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN x
ONBUILD MAINTAINER x
MAINTAINER a@b.c
COPY --from=0 / /
COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/
COPY a /dest
ADD app.js /app/
ADD app.tar.gz /app/
ADD https://example.com/f /app/
USER app
USER 1000:1000
USER $UID
ENV DB_PASSWORD=x
ENV A=1 NPM_TOKEN=y
ARG GITHUB_TOKEN
ARG VERSION=1
ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=x

rules.why:
The shell form runs the command as `/bin/sh -c "..."`, so the shell, not your program, is the main process of the container. `docker stop` sends SIGTERM to that shell, which usually does not pass it on; after the timeout (10 seconds by default) Docker kills the container with SIGKILL, and the program gets no chance to shut down cleanly. With an `ENTRYPOINT` in shell form, the arguments of `CMD` and of `docker run` are ignored as well.

The JSON form starts the program directly. If you need a shell, write `["sh", "-c", "exec node server.js"]`.

rules.description: Reports a stage whose last `USER` is root, on that `USER`. That is `root` or `0`, also `root:group` and `0:group`. Every stage is checked, build stages too. A stage with no `USER` instruction is not reported.

example.input:
FROM alpine
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM build
FROM scratch
FROM alpine:3 AS build
FROM $BASE
FROM alpine:3 AS Build
FROM BUILD
FROM localhost:5000/img
FROM localhost:5000/img:1
FROM alpine@sha256:abc
USER root
USER app
USER 0:0
COPY --from=build /a /b
COPY --from=nope /a /b
COPY --from=BUILD /a /b
COPY --from=0 /a /b
COPY --from=99 /a /b
COPY --from=alpine:3 /a /b
CMD ["a"]
CMD ["b"]
ENTRYPOINT ["a"]
ENTRYPOINT ["b"]
HEALTHCHECK CMD a
HEALTHCHECK CMD b
FROM alpine:3 AS last
COPY --from=LAST /a /b
USER app
CMD ["a"]
USER root

rules.why:
The container's main process runs as the last user. If the application is compromised, the attacker is root inside the container, which makes it easier to damage mounted volumes or to break out of the container, and files the process writes to a volume are owned by root.

End the stage with an unprivileged `USER` (a numeric one, see `numeric-user-id`).

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that could be merged into the `RUN` before it. Both are one simple command, with the same leading options (`--mount=...`). A comment between the two does not break the pair; any other instruction does. A `RUN` with `&&`, `;` or a pipe is neither reported nor part of a pair.

example.input:
FROM debian:12
RUN a
RUN b
# a comment between does not matter
RUN c
ENV A=1
RUN d
RUN e && f
RUN g
RUN h $(i)
RUN j
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/x k
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/x l
RUN m
RUN ["n", "o"]
RUN ["p"]

RUN a | b
RUN a || b
RUN ["a", "b"]
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]
RUN a | b
FROM debian:12
RUN a | b
RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y a
RUN apt update
RUN apt-get update && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y a && rm -fr "/var/lib/apt/lists"
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt/lists apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y a

upstream.note: Both RUNs must be a single command with the same flags.

rules.why:
Every `RUN` creates an image layer. Files that one `RUN` writes and the next one deletes (a download, a package cache) still sit in the earlier layer and count toward the image size; joined with `&&` in one `RUN`, the cleanup really removes them.

The price is a coarser build cache: when any part of the joined `RUN` changes, all of it runs again.

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that calls `apt`; use `apt-get` or `apt-cache` instead.

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN sudo make install
RUN cd /app && make
RUN service nginx start
RUN apt update
RUN wget https://example.com/f
RUN wget -q https://example.com/f
RUN ln -sf /bin/bash /bin/sh
RUN echo sudo cd ps
RUN make && \
    sudo make install
RUN v=$(sudo make) && echo "$(wget https://example.com/f)"
ONBUILD RUN sudo make
RUN ["sudo", "make"]

rules.why: `apt` is made for people at a terminal: its output and options may change between versions, and it prints a warning that it has no stable command line interface and should be used with caution in scripts. `apt-get` and `apt-cache` keep an interface that scripts can rely on.

rules.description: Reports a `COPY --from=stage / /`, which copies the whole file system of a stage to `/`. A copy of `/` into a folder (`/app/`) or of a folder is not reported.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch
FROM alpine:3@sha256:abc
WORKDIR app
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443
CMD node server.js
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
ENTRYPOINT /run.sh
ONBUILD CMD echo hi
ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN x
ONBUILD MAINTAINER x
MAINTAINER a@b.c
COPY --from=0 / /
COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/
COPY a /dest
ADD app.js /app/
ADD app.tar.gz /app/
ADD https://example.com/f /app/
USER app
USER 1000:1000
USER $UID
ENV DB_PASSWORD=x
ENV A=1 NPM_TOKEN=y
ARG GITHUB_TOKEN
ARG VERSION=1
ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=x

rules.why:
It copies everything of the build stage: compilers, package caches, sources, and the stage's own `/etc` and `/usr` over the ones of the final image. The image becomes as large as the build stage, which defeats the purpose of a multi-stage build, and files of the base image are overwritten.

Copy only what the final image needs: `COPY --from=build /out/app /usr/local/bin/`.

rules.description: Reports a `FROM` with a fixed `--platform`, such as `--platform=linux/amd64`. A value that contains `$BUILDPLATFORM` or `$TARGETPLATFORM` is not reported; other variables such as `$TARGETARCH` are.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch
FROM alpine:3@sha256:abc
WORKDIR app
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443
CMD node server.js
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
ENTRYPOINT /run.sh
ONBUILD CMD echo hi
ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN x
ONBUILD MAINTAINER x
MAINTAINER a@b.c
COPY --from=0 / /
COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/
COPY a /dest
ADD app.js /app/
ADD app.tar.gz /app/
ADD https://example.com/f /app/
USER app
USER 1000:1000
USER $UID
ENV DB_PASSWORD=x
ENV A=1 NPM_TOKEN=y
ARG GITHUB_TOKEN
ARG VERSION=1
ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=x

rules.why:
A fixed platform ties the build to one CPU architecture. On an arm64 machine the base image is pulled for amd64 and runs under emulation, which is slow and sometimes breaks, and a multi-platform build produces the same amd64 content for every target.

Without the option the base follows the platform of the build; a stage that must run on the build machine uses `--platform=$BUILDPLATFORM`.

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that calls `ssh`, `vim`, `shutdown`, `service`, `ps`, `free`, `top`, `kill` or `mount`.

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN sudo make install
RUN cd /app && make
RUN service nginx start
RUN apt update
RUN wget https://example.com/f
RUN wget -q https://example.com/f
RUN ln -sf /bin/bash /bin/sh
RUN echo sudo cd ps
RUN make && \
    sudo make install
RUN v=$(sudo make) && echo "$(wget https://example.com/f)"
ONBUILD RUN sudo make
RUN ["sudo", "make"]

rules.why: A build runs without a terminal and without an init system, and each `RUN` ends when its command returns. `ssh`, `vim` and `top` need a terminal. `service` and `shutdown` talk to an init system that the container does not have; a daemon started by `service` stops when that `RUN` ends, so it is not running in containers of the image. `ps`, `free`, `kill` and `mount` report on or change the temporary build sandbox, and nothing of it lasts.

rules.description: Reports a `FROM` whose image has the tag `latest` (`alpine:latest`). A `latest` image with a digest (`alpine:latest@sha256:...`) is not reported; an image with no tag at all is the business of `untagged-base-image`.

FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch

WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443
CMD node server.js
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
ENTRYPOINT /run.sh
ONBUILD CMD echo hi
ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN x
ONBUILD MAINTAINER x
MAINTAINER a@b.c
COPY --from=0 / /
COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/
COPY a /dest
ADD app.js /app/
ADD app.tar.gz /app/
ADD https://example.com/f /app/
USER app
USER 1000:1000
USER $UID
ENV DB_PASSWORD=x
ENV A=1 NPM_TOKEN=y
ARG GITHUB_TOKEN
ARG VERSION=1

rules.why:
`latest` is only a name that the image's owner moves to each new release. The base of your image then changes without any edit in the Dockerfile: a rebuild can pull a new major version of the operating system or runtime, and a build that worked yesterday fails or behaves differently today.

A release tag (`alpine:3.20`) or a digest keeps the base fixed.

Only the name is read, so `PASSWORD_FILE` and `PRIVATE_NET` are reported too, and the value is not looked at.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch

rules.why:

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that replaces `/bin/sh`. That is an `ln` command with `/bin/sh` among its arguments (`ln -sf /bin/bash /bin/sh`).

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN sudo make install
RUN cd /app && make
RUN service nginx start
RUN apt update
RUN wget https://example.com/f
RUN wget -q https://example.com/f
RUN ln -sf /bin/bash /bin/sh
RUN echo sudo cd ps
RUN make && \
    sudo make install
RUN v=$(sudo make) && echo "$(wget https://example.com/f)"
ONBUILD RUN sudo make
RUN ["sudo", "make"]

rules.why:
Replacing `/bin/sh` changes the shell that every script of the image, and of the packages you install, expects to be a POSIX `sh`. Scripts that start with `#!/bin/sh` then run under another shell than the one they were written for, and package scripts can fail in odd ways.

To use another shell for the build, the `SHELL` instruction (`SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]`) changes only the shell of the later `RUN` instructions.

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that calls `sudo`.

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN sudo make install
RUN cd /app && make
RUN service nginx start
RUN apt update
RUN wget https://example.com/f
RUN wget -q https://example.com/f
RUN ln -sf /bin/bash /bin/sh
RUN echo sudo cd ps
RUN make && \
    sudo make install
RUN v=$(sudo make) && echo "$(wget https://example.com/f)"
ONBUILD RUN sudo make
RUN ["sudo", "make"]

rules.why:
A `RUN` already runs as the user of the last `USER` instruction, root by default, so `sudo` adds nothing. Most images do not have it installed, and where it exists it may ask for a password or reset the environment (`HOME`, `PATH`), so the command sees something else than the rest of the build.

For a step that needs root, put `USER root` before it and switch back after it; to drop privileges at start, use a tool such as `gosu` in the entrypoint.

rules.description: Reports an `npm install` (also `npm i` and `npm add`) of a package without a version: `express` instead of `express@4.18.2`, `@scope/name` instead of `@scope/name@1.2.0`. A path, a tarball (`.tgz`, `.tar.gz`) or a git URL with a `#ref` counts as pinned. The value of `--loglevel` or `--registry` is not taken for a package, and an `npm install` with no package (it reads `package.json`) is not reported.

example.input:
FROM node:20
RUN pip install flask
RUN pip install flask==2.0 "requests>=2"
RUN pip3 install -r requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -i https://x/simple flask==1
RUN pip install .
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b@v1
RUN npm install
RUN npm install express
RUN npm install express@4 @scope/pkg@1
RUN npm install --loglevel verbose express@4
RUN npm install ./local
RUN npm i express
RUN npm add express@4
RUN gem install rails
RUN gem install --no-document rails
RUN gem install --source https://rubygems.org rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails -v 7.0
RUN go install example.com/x
RUN go install example.com/x@v1
RUN go install example.com/x@latest

upstream.note: A package is judged by its text (`@`, `#`, tarball, path); git and scoped forms follow hadolint's cases only.

rules.why:
Without a version npm installs the latest release on the day of the build, so a new major version of the package can break the image and two builds of one Dockerfile differ.

Pin the version in the command, or keep it in `package.json` with a lock file and use `npm ci`.

rules.description: Reports a `USER` whose user is a name instead of a number (`USER app`, `USER app:1000`). `USER 1000`, `USER 1000:app` and a variable are not reported: only the user part is checked, the group may be a name.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch
FROM alpine:3@sha256:abc
WORKDIR app
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443
CMD node server.js
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
ENTRYPOINT /run.sh
ONBUILD CMD echo hi
ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN x
ONBUILD MAINTAINER x
MAINTAINER a@b.c
COPY --from=0 / /
COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/
COPY a /dest
ADD app.js /app/
ADD app.tar.gz /app/
ADD https://example.com/f /app/
USER app
USER 1000:1000
USER $UID
ENV DB_PASSWORD=x
ENV A=1 NPM_TOKEN=y
ARG GITHUB_TOKEN
ARG VERSION=1
ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=x

upstream.note: A variable is accepted whether or not an ARG defines it.

rules.why:
A name is looked up in the `/etc/passwd` of the image at run time, which tools outside the image cannot do. Kubernetes with `runAsNonRoot: true` refuses to start a container whose image user is a name (it cannot verify that the user is not root), and file permissions on mounted volumes use the number, not the name.

Create the user with a fixed id (`useradd -u 1000 app`) and write `USER 1000`.

rules.description:
Reports a `pip install` (also `pip3`, `pip3.12`) of a package without a version. A package is pinned when it has a specifier (`==`, `>=`, `<`, `!=`, `~=`) or is a wheel, a source archive or a path (`.whl`, `.tar.gz`, anything with a `/`). A VCS requirement such as `git+https://example.com/x.git` must name a revision after `@`.

Not reported: `pip install -r requirements.txt` and `-c constraints.txt` (the versions are in the file), `pip install .`, and the values of options such as `-i`, `-e` or `-t`. `python -m pip install` and `pipenv` are not checked.

example.input:
FROM node:20
RUN pip install flask
RUN pip install flask==2.0 "requests>=2"
RUN pip3 install -r requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -i https://x/simple flask==1
RUN pip install .
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b
RUN pip install git+https://github.com/a/b@v1
RUN npm install
RUN npm install express
RUN npm install express@4 @scope/pkg@1
RUN npm install --loglevel verbose express@4
RUN npm install ./local
RUN npm i express
RUN npm add express@4
RUN gem install rails
RUN gem install --no-document rails
RUN gem install --source https://rubygems.org rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails:7.0
RUN gem install rails -v 7.0
RUN go install example.com/x
RUN go install example.com/x@v1
RUN go install example.com/x@latest

upstream.note: `python -m pip install` and the wrappers (`pipx`, `pipenv`) are not told apart as hadolint does.

rules.why:
An unpinned `pip install` takes the latest release of the package, and of the libraries it depends on, on the day of the build. A new major version can break the application, and two builds of one Dockerfile give different images.

Pin the packages, ideally in a `requirements.txt` made by a lock tool, and install it with `-r`.

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` with a pipe (`a | b`) in a stage whose `SHELL` does not set `pipefail`. No earlier `SHELL` instruction of the stage has a word that contains `pipefail` (`SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]`). A `set -o pipefail` inside the `RUN` itself does not count. A new `FROM` starts the check again.

example.input:
FROM debian:12
RUN a
RUN b
# a comment between does not matter
RUN c
ENV A=1
RUN d
RUN e && f
RUN g
RUN h $(i)
RUN j
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/x k
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/x l
RUN m
RUN ["n", "o"]
RUN ["p"]

RUN a | b
RUN a || b
RUN ["a", "b"]
SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]
RUN a | b
FROM debian:12
RUN a | b
RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y a
RUN apt update
RUN apt-get update && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y a && rm -fr "/var/lib/apt/lists"
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt/lists apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y a

upstream.note: A SHELL instruction with a word that contains `pipefail` ends the check for the rest of the stage.

rules.why:
The exit status of a pipe is the one of its last command. `curl -f https://example.com/x | tar xz` succeeds even when curl fails and tar gets nothing, so the build goes on with a missing or broken file and the error shows up much later. With `pipefail` any failing command of the pipe fails the `RUN`.

To fix, set the option for the stage with `SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]`; the default `/bin/sh` of some images (Debian's dash) does not have the option.

rules.description: Reports a `yum install`, `dnf install` or `microdnf install` of a package without a version. A package is pinned when it is written `name-version` (`curl-7.88.1`: a digit after a dash), is a `.rpm` file or contains a variable. Commands with `module` or `group` are not checked.

RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && yum clean all
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && rm -rf /var/cache/yum/*

RUN zypper install -y curl=7.0 && zypper clean
RUN zypper install -y curl
RUN zypper dist-upgrade
RUN zypper -n in curl=1 && zypper cc

upstream.note: A variable in a package counts as pinned; hadolint checks that an ENV or ARG defines it.
A variable in a package counts as pinned; hadolint checks that an ENV or ARG defines it.

rules.why:
An unpinned install takes the newest version in the enabled repositories on the day of the build. Two builds of one Dockerfile can then differ, and a new release can break the image without any change in your code.

Pinned versions make the build repeatable. Repositories drop old versions, so a pin needs updating from time to time.

rules.description: Reports each `CMD` after the first one in the same stage. A `CMD` after `ONBUILD` is not counted, and a new `FROM` starts the count again.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest

FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3

rules.description: Reports each `ENTRYPOINT` after the first one in the same stage. An `ENTRYPOINT` after `ONBUILD` is not counted, and a new `FROM` starts the count again.

FROM build
FROM scratch

FROM $BASE

rules.description: Reports each `HEALTHCHECK` after the first one in the same stage, `HEALTHCHECK NONE` included. A new `FROM` starts the count again.

rules.description: Reports a `FROM` image with neither a tag nor a digest (`FROM alpine`). Docker reads it as `:latest`. Not reported: `scratch`, a variable (`$BASE`) and the name of an earlier stage (compared without case). A `:` in the registry host (`localhost:5000/app`) is a port, not a tag.

FROM scratch

ENTRYPOINT ["b"]

rules.why:
An image without a tag is pulled as `latest`, so the Dockerfile does not even say which version it builds on. The base changes with each upstream release, and a rebuild can fail or behave differently with no change in the file.

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that calls `cd`, anywhere in its script (also in a subshell such as `(cd sub && make)`).

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN sudo make install
RUN cd /app && make
RUN service nginx start
RUN apt update
RUN wget https://example.com/f
RUN wget -q https://example.com/f
RUN ln -sf /bin/bash /bin/sh
RUN echo sudo cd ps
RUN make && \
    sudo make install
RUN v=$(sudo make) && echo "$(wget https://example.com/f)"
ONBUILD RUN sudo make
RUN ["sudo", "make"]

rules.why:
`cd` changes the directory for that one `RUN`; the next instruction starts again in the `WORKDIR`, so it is easy to believe you are in a directory you are not in.

`WORKDIR` states the directory once, creates it when it is missing, and applies to every later `RUN`, `CMD`, `ENTRYPOINT`, `COPY` and `ADD`.

rules.description: Reports a `wget` call that does not limit its progress output. It has none of `--progress`, `-q` or `--quiet`, `-nv` or `--no-verbose`, `-o` or `--output-file`, `-a` or `--append-output`.

example.input:
FROM alpine:3
RUN sudo make install
RUN cd /app && make
RUN service nginx start
RUN apt update
RUN wget https://example.com/f
RUN wget -q https://example.com/f
RUN ln -sf /bin/bash /bin/sh
RUN echo sudo cd ps
RUN make && \
    sudo make install
RUN v=$(sudo make) && echo "$(wget https://example.com/f)"
ONBUILD RUN sudo make
RUN ["sudo", "make"]

rules.why:
By default wget draws a progress bar. A build is not a terminal, so each update is logged as a line of its own, and a large download adds thousands of lines to the build log. The log gets hard to read and CI logs reach their size limits.

`--progress=dot:giga`, `-nv` or `-q` keep the output short.

rules.description: Reports a `WORKDIR` with a relative path. A path is absolute when it starts with `/`, a drive letter (`C:`) or a variable (`$HOME`, `${DIR}/x`). Quotes around the path make no difference, and a relative path is reported also after an absolute `WORKDIR`.

example.input:
FROM alpine:latest
FROM --platform=linux/amd64 alpine:3
FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM alpine:3
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM alpine:3 AS scratch
FROM alpine:3@sha256:abc
WORKDIR app
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR $HOME
EXPOSE 8080 70000
EXPOSE 80/tcp 443
CMD node server.js
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
ENTRYPOINT /run.sh
ONBUILD CMD echo hi
ONBUILD ONBUILD RUN x
ONBUILD MAINTAINER x
MAINTAINER a@b.c
COPY --from=0 / /
COPY a b /dest
COPY a b /dest/
COPY a /dest
ADD app.js /app/
ADD app.tar.gz /app/
ADD https://example.com/f /app/
USER app
USER 1000:1000
USER $UID
ENV DB_PASSWORD=x
ENV A=1 NPM_TOKEN=y
ARG GITHUB_TOKEN
ARG VERSION=1
ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=x
