rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that installs with yum and does not clean the cache. It runs `yum install` and has no `yum clean all` after it in the same `RUN`. An `rm -rf /var/cache/yum/*` written exactly so is accepted as well.

example.input:
FROM fedora:40
RUN yum install curl
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && yum clean all
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && rm -rf /var/cache/yum/*
RUN yum install -y nginx-1.2 && yum clean all
RUN dnf install curl
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0 && dnf clean all
RUN microdnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y ./a.rpm && dnf clean all
RUN zypper install curl
RUN zypper install -y curl=7.0 && zypper clean
RUN zypper install -y curl
RUN zypper dist-upgrade
RUN zypper -n in curl=1 && zypper cc

rules.why:
`yum install` stores the metadata and packages it downloaded under `/var/cache/yum`. That cache is written into the layer and stays in the image, adding size that nothing uses at run time.

Clean it in the same `RUN`: a later `RUN` cannot shrink a layer that was already written.

rules.description: Reports a `yum install`, `yum groupinstall` or `yum localinstall` without `-y` or `--assumeyes`.

example.input:
FROM fedora:40
RUN yum install curl
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && yum clean all
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && rm -rf /var/cache/yum/*
RUN yum install -y nginx-1.2 && yum clean all
RUN dnf install curl
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0 && dnf clean all
RUN microdnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y ./a.rpm && dnf clean all
RUN zypper install curl
RUN zypper install -y curl=7.0 && zypper clean
RUN zypper install -y curl
RUN zypper dist-upgrade
RUN zypper -n in curl=1 && zypper cc

rules.why: Before it installs, yum asks `Is this ok [y/N]`. A build has no terminal to answer, so yum reads the missing answer as no, exits with an error, and the `RUN` fails.

rules.description: Reports a `RUN` that installs with zypper and does not clean the cache. It runs `zypper install` (`in`) and has no `zypper clean` or `zypper cc` after it in the same `RUN`. A `RUN` with a `--mount` of type `cache` or `tmpfs` on `/var/cache/zypp` is not reported.

example.input:
FROM fedora:40
RUN yum install curl
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && yum clean all
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && rm -rf /var/cache/yum/*
RUN yum install -y nginx-1.2 && yum clean all
RUN dnf install curl
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0 && dnf clean all
RUN microdnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y ./a.rpm && dnf clean all
RUN zypper install curl
RUN zypper install -y curl=7.0 && zypper clean
RUN zypper install -y curl
RUN zypper dist-upgrade
RUN zypper -n in curl=1 && zypper cc

rules.why:
`zypper install` stores the metadata and packages it downloaded under `/var/cache/zypp`. That cache is written into the layer and stays in the image, adding size that nothing uses at run time.

Clean it in the same `RUN`: a later `RUN` cannot shrink a layer that was already written.

rules.description: Reports a `zypper dist-upgrade` (or `dup`).

example.input:
FROM fedora:40
RUN yum install curl
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && yum clean all

RUN yum install -y nginx-1.2 && yum clean all

RUN dnf install -y ./a.rpm && dnf clean all
RUN zypper install curl
RUN zypper install -y curl=7.0 && zypper clean

RUN zypper dist-upgrade
RUN zypper -n in curl=1 && zypper cc

rules.why:
A distribution upgrade moves every package to the newest version of the enabled repositories, possibly into a new distribution release. The image is then no longer the release that the base image's tag names, and two builds can end in different states.

Use `zypper update` to apply fixes within the release, or move to a newer base image.

rules.description: Reports a `zypper install` (`in`) of a package without a version. A package is pinned when its name has `=`, `<` or `>` (`curl=7.88.1`) or when it is a `.rpm` file.

example.input:
FROM fedora:40
RUN yum install curl
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && yum clean all
RUN yum install -y curl-7.0 && rm -rf /var/cache/yum/*
RUN yum install -y nginx-1.2 && yum clean all

RUN dnf install -y curl-7.0

RUN microdnf install -y curl-7.0
RUN dnf install -y ./a.rpm && dnf clean all
RUN zypper install curl
RUN zypper install -y curl=7.0 && zypper clean

RUN zypper dist-upgrade

rules.why:
An unpinned install takes the newest version in the enabled repositories on the day of the build. Two builds of one Dockerfile can then differ, and a new release can break the image without any change in your code.

Pinned versions make the build repeatable. Repositories drop old versions, so a pin needs updating from time to time.

rules.description: The first line of the doc comment of an exported function, method, type, constant or variable does not start with its name (revive exported). A type may start with `A`, `An`, `The` or `This` before the name. The comment of a group in parentheses is the comment of its types; a constant or variable in a group whose comment has text is not checked. rules.description: A package-level `var` of one name made by `errors.New` or `fmt.Errorf` starts with `err`, or `Err` when exported.
rules.why: A package-level error variable is a sentinel that callers compare against with `errors.Is`, and it is read from other packages. The `err` and `Err` prefixes make such variables recognizable at the use site and keep the exported ones apart from other exported names. It is a Go convention; nothing breaks without it.

rules.description: The text of an error made with `fmt.Errorf`, `errors.New`, `errors.Errorf`, `errors.Wrap` and the like ends in `.`, `:`, `!` or a newline (a capital first letter is not reported). The text is the first argument, or the second of the functions that wrap an error (`errors.Wrap(err, "failed.")`).
rules.why: Error strings are joined into longer messages (`failed to open: ` plus the cause), so a full stop, colon, exclamation mark or newline at the end leaves a doubled or dangling mark in the result and in logs. The Go code review comments ask for messages without end punctuation.

rules.description: `errors.New(fmt.Sprintf(...))` is `fmt.Errorf(...)` (the `t.Error(fmt.Sprintf(...))` form on a `*testing.T` needs types and is not read).

example.input:
package a

func f() {
	_ = errors.New(fmt.Sprintf("x %d", 1))
	_ = errors.New(fmt.Sprint("x"), 1)
	_ = errors.New("x")
	_ = fmt.Errorf("x %d", 1)
	_ = errors.New(fmt.Sprintf("x") + "y")
}

rules.why:
`fmt.Errorf` formats and wraps (`%w`) in one call, and `go vet` knows its format string. `errors.New(fmt.Sprintf(...))` formats a string first and then wraps it in an error, which is longer and cannot wrap another error with `%w`.

To fix, call `fmt.Errorf` with the same format and arguments.

rules.description: `x += 1` and `x -= 1`, where `x++` and `x--` say the same. Only the literal `1` counts. Left out of a language that has no `++`.
rules.why: `x++` and `x--` are the short forms of `x += 1` and `x -= 1` and are what readers look for in a loop or a counter. Using one form everywhere makes counters easy to find. The rule is off by default because the long form is a valid style in some codebases.

rules.description: An `else` block after an `if` block that ends in `return`: the code of the `else` can follow the `if`. An `else if` is left alone.
rules.why:
When the `if` block ends in `return`, the `else` only adds a level of indentation to the code that follows. Without it the normal path stays at the left edge and the early return reads as a guard, which is the Go way of handling errors first. Removing the `else` does not change what the function does.

To fix, delete `else` and move its block after the `if`.

upstream.note: Only more than one capital in a row; no allowed length or ignore options.

rules.description: An array creation whose `{` follows the `]` right away, `new int[]{1}` (Checkstyle ArrayBracketNoWhitespace).

upstream.note: Only the `{` of an array creation right after the `]`.

rules.description: A declarator or parameter with C-style brackets after the name (Checkstyle ArrayTypeStyle).

A string or character literal writes a visible character as a `\uXXXX` escape, and the line has no trailing comment (Checkstyle AvoidEscapedUnicodeCharacters). Escapes of control, space and format characters are fine.

upstream.note: Printable-escape rule with control characters and tail comments allowed; no options.

rules.description: A line of a Javadoc comment after the first starts with an asterisk (Checkstyle JavadocMissingLeadingAsterisk). Empty lines are left alone.

The paragraphs of a Javadoc comment: a `

` tag stands right before the first word of its paragraph (no space) and after an empty line, an empty line between paragraphs is followed by `

`, and the comment does not start with `

` (Checkstyle JavadocParagraph). Text inside `

`, `
    ` and the like, and after the first block tag, is left alone.

example.input:
/** * Good. * *

Fine paragraph. * *

Space after. * * Missing tag. *

Not after an empty line. * *

    *
  • item *
* * {@snippet : * code(); * * more(); * } * * 
 *
 * kept
 *
* * @param x text * * after the tags */ class A { /**

First thing. */ void f() {} }

upstream.note:
`

` and empty-line placement; not `allowNewlineParagraph`.

rules.description: A Javadoc comment starts with a summary: a first sentence that ends with a period (followed by a blank or the end of the text) and does not start with a forbidden fragment (Checkstyle SummaryJavadoc). A comment of `{@inheritDoc}` or `{@return ...}` needs none.

options.description: Regular expression a summary must not match at its start; empty: no check.
options.name: forbidden_fragments

upstream.note: Period and forbidden fragments; the summary is read from the lines of the comment, not from parsed HTML.

rules.description: A line that continues a block tag (`@param x`) is indented by at least `indent` blanks after the asterisk (Checkstyle JavadocTagContinuationIndentation: its offset of 4 is 5 blanks here). Lines that start HTML and lines inside `<pre>` and the like are left alone.

example.input:
/** * Summary. * * @param a first * continued with one blank * @param b first * continued with five blanks * @param c first * four blanks are not enough * @return x * 
 *   html is left alone
 *
*/ class A {}

options.description: Blanks after the asterisk that a continuation line needs.
options.name: indent

rules.description: A `;` that is the body of an `if` or a loop, such as `while (x);` (Checkstyle EmptyStatement).

upstream.note: Only the body of an `if` or a loop.

rules.description: A class body that declares `boolean equals(Object)` and no `hashCode()`: equal objects get different hash codes (Checkstyle EqualsHashCode).

upstream.note: Only `equals` without `hashCode`, not the reverse.

rules.description: A string or character literal writes backspace, tab, line feed, form feed, carriage return, a quote or a backslash as an octal or unicode escape (Checkstyle IllegalTokenText).

upstream.note: Only the special-escape message of the Google config.

rules.description: A `switch` statement with no `default` (Checkstyle MissingSwitchDefault).

Reports a `case` whose statements can reach the next `case` or `default`, and an empty one that is followed by a blank line, without a comment that says `falls through` before the next one (or at the end of its block). Cases that stack with no statement between them (`case 1: case 2: b();`) are not reported.
rules.why:
Execution that runs on from one case into the next is easily a forgotten `break`: the reader cannot tell it from an error, and the code of the second case then runs for the first value too.

To fix, end the case with `break` or `return`; if the fall-through is meant, write a `// falls through` comment.

rules.description: A parameter is assigned a new value (Checkstyle ParameterAssignment). No fix.
`==` or `!=` with a string literal as an operand compares references (Checkstyle StringLiteralEquality).
A line of a comment starts with `todo` in any other case, or with `TODO` and no colon (Checkstyle TodoComment with the Google format). Javadoc comments are not read.

upstream.note: The Google format only, no option.
The check id of the Google TodoComment instance.

rules.description: An import whose name the file does not use (Checkstyle UnusedImports, ktlint no-unused-imports). Imports with `*` are not checked, and a name in a doc comment counts as a use where the language has doc comments. No fix: removing an import can change which declaration a name means.

upstream.note: Names in Javadoc count as used; no option to turn that off.

rules.description: A local variable that is never read: it is declared, and perhaps assigned, and that is all (Checkstyle UnusedLocalVariable, RuboCop Lint/UselessAssignment). No fix.

upstream.note: not an assignment that is overwritten before any read

rules.description: An integer literal that ends in a lower case `l` (Checkstyle UpperEll).

Reports an overload (a signature or function with the same name as an earlier one) with another member between it and the earlier overloads. It checks interface and class members, call and construct signatures, and function declarations.
rules.why:
Overloads are read together as one declaration with several shapes. When another member sits between them, a reader can miss one shape or take a later signature for an unrelated member.

To fix, move the overloads next to each other.

rules.description: Reports `Array<T>`, `ReadonlyArray<T>` and `Readonly<T[]>` written as generic types, each level of a nested one (`Array<Array<number>>` is two reports). The bare `Array` is not reported.

upstream.note: only the default `array` style (`default` and `readonly` options); a local type named `Array` is still reported

rules.why:
Two spellings of one type make code harder to scan and search; the bracket form `T[]` is shorter and reads left to right.

To fix, write `T[]` and `readonly T[]`.

rules.description: Reports a `@ts-ignore` comment, a `@ts-nocheck` comment before the first statement, and a `@ts-expect-error` comment whose description is shorter than three characters (`// @ts-expect-error: the API types are wrong` is fine). Line and block comments are read. `@ts-check` is not reported.

upstream.note: the options (`minimumDescriptionLength`, per-directive settings, `descriptionFormat`) keep their defaults

rules.why:
`@ts-ignore` hides every type error on the next line and keeps hiding them after the code changes, so a later, real error on that line is never shown. `@ts-nocheck` turns checking off for the whole file. `@ts-expect-error` is safer, because the compiler complains when the error is gone, but without a reason nobody knows when it is safe to remove.

To fix, remove the error with a proper type, or use `@ts-expect-error` with a short reason.

rules.description: Reports a type alias of an object type (`type T = { a: 1 }`, also `{}` and an index signature type). A union, an intersection or any other type in an alias is not reported.

upstream.note: only the default `interface` style

rules.why:
An `interface` and an object type alias describe the same shape, but interfaces can be extended and merged, and the compiler reports their errors with the name of the interface instead of the expanded type. One form in a code base is easier to search.

To fix, write `interface T { a: 1 }`.

rules.description: Reports an import in a TypeScript file whose names are all used only as types (also in `typeof` of a type) and is not written `import type`, a mixed import with such a name (the value names stay in an `import`), and the type form `import("a").B`. A name that is not used at all is not reported.

upstream.note: the options keep their defaults (`prefer` type-imports, `fixStyle` separate-type-imports); `emitDecoratorMetadata` is not known, so a file with decorators is checked

rules.why:
An import used only for types is erased when the file is compiled, but the compiler cannot always know that, so a plain `import` may stay as a real load with side effects, and a cycle between files can appear that the types did not need. `import type` states it, so the import is always removed.

To fix, write `import type { T } from 'x'` or `import { type T } from 'x'`.

rules.description: Reports a getter written with `get name() {}` (in a class or an object literal) that does not return a value on every path: an empty body, a `return;` without a value, or an `if` without `else` that returns only in one branch. A getter that always throws is not reported, and neither is a `get` function given to `Object.defineProperty`.

upstream.note: the getters of Object.defineProperty and Reflect.defineProperty descriptors are not checked

rules.why:
A property read calls the getter and takes its result, so a path without a value makes the property `undefined`, usually by a forgotten `return` rather than by intent.

To fix, return a value on every path.

rules.description: Reports `new Promise(async ...)`: an `async` function (or arrow function) as the executor, with or without a second argument.
rules.why:
The `Promise` constructor ignores what its executor returns. An error thrown in an `async` executor rejects the promise the executor returned, which nobody holds, so the new promise never settles and the caller waits forever; the error shows up only as an unhandled rejection, if at all.

To fix, give the executor as a normal function and call `resolve` and `reject` yourself, or drop `new Promise` and write an `async` function that returns the value.

rules.description: Reports a `let`, `const`, `using`, function or class declared directly in a `case` or `default` clause. A declaration inside a block in the clause (`case 1: { let a; }`) is not reported, and neither is `var`.
rules.why:
A lexical declaration in a `case` clause is scoped to the whole `switch` block, not to the clause, so the other clauses can see the name and, when execution jumps over the declaration, reading it throws a `ReferenceError`. The code reads as if each clause had its own scope, and it does not.

To fix, put the body of the clause in braces: `case 1: { let b = 1; break; }`.

rules.description: Reports an assignment to a class that is declared by name (`class K {} K = 1;`).
rules.why:
A class declaration creates a binding, and replacing it means the name stops standing for the class: later code that uses the name (`new K()`) gets something else, and the class is no longer reachable by that name.

To fix, assign to another variable, or declare the class with `let K = class {}` where reassigning is intended.

rules.description: Reports a comparison with `-0` on either side of `==`, `!=`, `===`, `!==`, `<`, `<=`, `>` or `>=`. `Object.is(x, -0)` and a comparison with `+0` are not reported.
rules.why:
`-0` and `0` are different values but compare as equal: `0 === -0` is `true`. So `x === -0` is also true for plain zero, and the check does not do what it reads like.

To fix, use `Object.is(x, -0)`, which tells them apart.

rules.description: Reports a write to a `const` variable after its declaration: an assignment, `++` or `--`, or a destructuring target (`[c] = [1]`). The initializer is not a write.
rules.why:
Assigning to a `const` throws a `TypeError` when the line runs, so the program fails where the change was meant.

To fix, declare the variable with `let`, or stop reassigning it.

rules.description: Reports a statement or a call that stops the program in a debugger: a `debugger;` statement, a call of one of the `calls` of the language (Python `breakpoint()`, `pdb.set_trace()`), or an import matching the option `imports`. A language lists its calls in its grammar's `rule` row.

options.description: Calls that start a debugger
options.name: calls

options.description: An import of a debugger module
options.name: imports

rules.why:
A debugger call left in the code stops the program for whoever runs it, and in production it hangs a request or a process. It is always a leftover.

To fix, delete the statement.

rules.description: Reports `delete` applied to a plain variable name, also in parentheses (`delete x`, `delete (x)`). `delete x.y` and `delete x[0]` remove a property and are not reported.
rules.why:
`delete` removes object properties, not variables. On a variable it does nothing in sloppy mode (the expression is `false`) and is a syntax error in strict mode and in modules, so the code either has no effect or does not run.

To fix, assign `undefined` to the variable or leave the scope, or delete the property of an object instead.

rules.description: Reports a class member whose name is already used by another member of the class: two methods, two fields, a field and a method, two getters. A getter with its setter may share a name, and so may a `static` and an instance member.
rules.why:
When two members have one name, the later one silently replaces the earlier, so the first body is dead code. It is usually a copy-paste mistake where the second member was meant to have another name.

To fix, rename one of them or delete the one that is not used.

rules.description: Reports an `else if` whose condition cannot be true at that point: it repeats a condition of an earlier branch of the chain (`if (a) {} else if (a) {}`), or each operand of its `||` is a whole earlier condition or an operand of an earlier `||` (`if (a || b) {} else if (a) {}`). A condition that is only implied by an earlier one (`a && b` after `a`) is not found.
rules.why:
If an earlier condition was true its branch ran, and if it was false the same condition is false again, so the later branch never runs. This is nearly always a copy-paste slip where the condition was not changed, and the code the author meant to run is the dead one.

To fix, correct the condition or remove the branch.

rules.description: Reports an enum member initialised with a string or number that an earlier member of the same enum already has (`A = 0, B = 0`). Computed values (`1 + 1`) are not compared.
rules.why:
Two names for one value make a value to name lookup (the reverse mapping of a numeric enum) answer with the later one, and the second member is usually a copy-paste mistake with the value not changed.

To fix, give the member its own value.

rules.description: Reports an `else` when the `if` and every `else if` before it end in `return` (what the `else` itself holds does not matter). An `else if` is not reported, and neither is a chain in which one of the earlier branches can fall through.

upstream.note: the allowElseIf option and the skip for an else that declares names are not supported; one extra report in the three.js corpus (98 matched)

rules.why:
When every earlier branch returns, the code in the `else` can follow the `if` without the `else`, which removes one level of nesting and makes the early return plain.

To fix, delete the `else` and de-indent its body.

rules.description: Reports `[]` in a regex literal. `[^]` (any character) and a `[]` in the string given to `new RegExp` are not reported.
rules.why:
A character class with no members can match nothing, so a regex that contains it never matches. It is nearly always an escape that was forgotten (`\[\]` meant) or a class whose content was deleted.

To fix, add the characters, or escape the brackets.

rules.description: Reports the type `{}` (also in `type T = {}`) and an interface with no members that extends at most one type. `{}` in an intersection (`{} & X`) and an interface that extends two types are not reported.

upstream.note: the options (`allowInterfaces`, `allowObjectTypes`, `allowWithName`) keep their defaults

rules.why:
`{}` does not mean an empty object: it accepts every value except `null` and `undefined`, numbers and strings included. An empty interface that only extends one type is the same as that type.

To fix, write `object` for any non-primitive, `unknown` for any value, `Record<string, never>` for an empty object, or the type itself.

rules.description: Reports a destructuring pattern with nothing in it: `{}` or `[]` in a declaration, a parameter, an assignment target or nested in another pattern (`var {a: {}} = x`). A default value in a pattern (`{a = {}}`) is not an empty pattern.
rules.why:
An empty pattern binds no name, so the statement does nothing but check that the value is not `null` or `undefined`. It is usually a mistake for a default value: `function f({a: {}}) {}` was meant to be `function f({a = {}}) {}`, and the parameter stays without a default.

To fix, write the names to bind, or the default with `=`.

rules.description: Reports the `any` type wherever a type is written (`let a: any`, `any[]`, a constraint such as `T extends any`).

upstream.note: the options (`ignoreRestArgs`, `fixToUnknown`) keep their defaults

rules.why:
`any` turns off type checking for everything that touches the value, and the value spreads: a call result, a property and an assignment of an `any` are `any` too, so one hole hides errors far from where it is written.

To fix, use `unknown` (it must be checked before use) or a real type.

rules.description: Reports `!!x` and `Boolean(x)` in a place that already converts the value to a boolean: the test of `if`, `while`, `do ... while`, `for` and `?:`, the operand of `!`, and the argument of `Boolean(...)`. `const b = !!x`, a call argument (`f(!!x)`) and `!!(x)` are not reported.

upstream.note: the `enforceForLogicalOperands` option is not supported

rules.why:
The cast changes nothing where the language already tests for truthiness, so it only adds noise and can suggest that the plain value is not allowed there. Where the real boolean is needed (an assignment, an argument), the cast does a job and is left alone.

To fix, remove the `!!` or the `Boolean(...)` call.

rules.description: Reports a second non-null assertion in a row (`a!!.b`) and a `!` right before an optional chain (`a!?.b`, `a!?.()`).
rules.why:
The second `!` of `a!!` changes nothing. In `a!?.b` the `!` says the value is not `null` while `?.` says it may be, so one of the two is wrong and the reader cannot tell which.

To fix, remove the extra `!`, or the `?.` if the value cannot be null.

rules.description: Reports an assignment to a function that is declared by name (`function f() {} f = 0;`), also `f++`.
rules.why:
A function declaration is hoisted, so calls above the assignment run the original and calls below run the new value. The name then means two things in one scope, and the declaration reads as the only definition.

To fix, assign to another variable, or declare the function with `let f = function () {}` where reassigning is intended.

rules.description: Reports a write to an imported name (`import a from 'a'; a = 1`, `bb = 2`), and a write to a member of a namespace import (`ns.x = 1`), a `delete ns.y` and `Object.assign(ns, {})`.
rules.why:
Imports are read-only live views of the exporting module. Assigning to one throws a `TypeError` in module code, and the namespace object of `import * as ns` cannot be changed either.

To fix, keep the value in a local variable, or let the exporting module offer a function that changes it.

rules.description: Reports a type annotation on a variable, parameter or class property whose initial value already gives that type (`const a: number = 5`, `s: string = 'x'`, `b: boolean = true`, `n: bigint = 1n`). A value from a call, a `readonly` property and an optional property are not reported.

example.input:
let a: "a" = "a", b: "a" = 'a', c: 1 = 1, d: string = "a";
class C { p: "a" = "a"; q = 1 as 1; r = <"a">"a"; s = "a" as "b"; }

upstream.note: the options (`ignoreParameters`, `ignoreProperties`) keep their defaults

rules.why:
The compiler infers the same type from the value, so the annotation only adds a second place to keep in sync.

To fix, drop the annotation.

rules.description: Reports unusual whitespace characters: vertical tab, form feed, no-break space (U+00A0), the spaces and zero-width characters U+2000 to U+200B, line and paragraph separators, narrow no-break space, medium mathematical space, ideographic space, and a byte order mark that is not at the start of the file. A string literal is not checked (the character is data there); comments, template literals and regex literals are. A run of them is one report.
rules.why:
These characters look like a space (or like nothing) but are different characters: a search for a space does not find them, a diff shows no change, and in code outside a string or comment some of them make the file fail to parse. They usually arrive by copying text from a web page or a document.

To fix, replace them with an ordinary space, or write the character as an escape (`\u00a0`) where it is wanted.

rules.description: Reports an `if` that is the only statement of an `else` block (`else { if (b) { ... } }`), also when that `if` has its own `else`. An `else` block with other statements, and an `if` inside an `else if`, are not reported.
rules.why:
`else { if (b) ... }` is the same as `else if (b) ...` and has one more level of nesting and braces for the reader to follow.

To fix, write `else if`.

rules.description: Reports a number literal that the 64-bit double it becomes does not hold exactly: `9007199254740993` (above 2^53), `0x20000000000001`, a value that is too large (`1e400`, becomes `Infinity`) or too small (`2e-400`, becomes `0`). `9007199254740992`, `0.1`, a number that has an exact double (`1e20`) and BigInt literals (`123n`) are not reported.
rules.why:
JavaScript rounds such a literal when the file is read, so the program computes with another number than the one written, with no error. Integers above 2^53 lose their last digits, which breaks ids and counters.

To fix, use a BigInt literal (`9007199254740993n`), keep the value in a string, or write the number the double really holds.

rules.description: Reports `new` and `constructor` declarations that do not describe a constructor: a class method signature `new(): C;` without a body that returns the class itself, an interface signature `new (): I` that returns the interface itself, and an interface member named `constructor()`. A class method named `new` with a body is not reported.
rules.why:
An interface cannot be constructed, so `new (): I` inside `interface I` describes a constructor that does not exist, and an interface member `constructor()` is only a method with that name, not a constructor. The code reads as a constructor but is not one.

To fix, declare the constructor in the class (`constructor()`), or put the `new` signature on a separate interface that types the constructor.

rules.description: Reports a `namespace N {}` or `module N {}` declaration, also a dotted `namespace A.B {}`. `declare module "x"`, `declare global`, and any namespace in a `.d.ts` file are not reported.

upstream.note: the option `allowDeclarations` keeps its default

rules.why:
A TypeScript namespace is an older way to group code that does not exist in JavaScript: it compiles to an object built by a function, cannot be tree-shaken well and is not understood by tools that only strip types. ES modules do the same grouping and are the standard.

To fix, move the members to a module file and `export` them.

rules.description: Reports a non-null assertion on the end of an optional chain: `a?.b!` and `(a?.b)!`. `a?.b!.c` is not reported.
rules.why:
An optional chain returns `undefined` when `a` is missing, so asserting its result is not `undefined` contradicts the chain, and the program will fail at run time when the assumption is wrong.

To fix, handle the missing value, or drop `?.` if `a` cannot be null.

rules.description: Reports a non-null assertion (`a!`, `a!.b`) in a TypeScript file.
rules.why:
`a!` tells the compiler the value is not `null` or `undefined` without checking it. When the assumption is wrong the program fails at run time with a `TypeError`, in the place the type system was meant to protect.

To fix, check the value (`if (a)`) or use optional chaining (`a?.b`) and handle the missing case.

rules.description: Reports a number literal that starts with `0` followed by another digit, such as `017` or `08`. `0`, `0.5` and the modern forms `0o17`, `0x1F` and `0b11` are not reported.
rules.why:
A leading zero makes a legacy octal literal: `017` is 15, not 17. A literal such as `08` or `09` has a digit that is not octal, so it is read as the decimal 8 or 9, which hides the mistake. Both forms are syntax errors in strict mode and in modules.

To fix, drop the leading zero for a decimal number or write `0o17` for an octal one.

rules.description: Reports a call of `hasOwnProperty`, `isPrototypeOf` or `propertyIsEnumerable` made on an object itself: `obj.hasOwnProperty(k)`, `obj?.hasOwnProperty(k)` and `obj['hasOwnProperty'](k)`. Reading the property without a call, and `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, k)`, are not reported.
rules.why:
The method comes from the prototype chain, and the object may not have it. `Object.create(null)` objects have no `hasOwnProperty`, so the call throws, and data from outside (a parsed JSON with a key `"hasOwnProperty"`) can replace the method with its own value.

To fix, call it from the prototype: `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(obj, k)`, or use `Object.hasOwn(obj, k)` where the target supports it.

rules.description: Reports a call of the global `require(...)` and an `import x = require(...)`. A `require` that the file declares itself (a parameter, for example) is not reported.

upstream.note: the options (`allow`, `allowAsImport`) keep their defaults; a `require` the file declares itself is not reported

rules.why:
`require` is the CommonJS loader and is not typed like an import: the result is `any` unless a type is added, and bundlers and the compiler cannot always follow it. An `import` is checked by the type system and understood by tools.

To fix, use `import`.

rules.description: Reports a variable, function, class, parameter or function-expression name that is `NaN`, `Infinity`, `eval`, `arguments` or `undefined`. `var undefined;` without a value is not reported.

upstream.note: without scope analysis `var undefined;` is accepted whatever is assigned to it later

rules.why:
These names are read as the global values everywhere else in the program. A local called `undefined` or `NaN` changes what a test such as `x === undefined` means inside its scope, and a variable named `eval` or `arguments` is a syntax error in strict mode.

To fix, rename the variable.

rules.description: Reports a hole in an array literal, at the extra comma: `[1, , 2]` and `[, 1]`. A single trailing comma (`[1, ]`) is not a hole.
rules.why:
A hole is an index with no element. `[1, , 2]` has the length 3, and methods such as `forEach` and `map` skip the hole while `for` loops and spread read it as `undefined`, so the same array behaves differently depending on how it is read. It is nearly always a typo for a single comma.

To fix, remove the extra comma, or write `undefined` (or `null`) where a value is meant.

rules.description: Reports `const self = this`, `let self = this` and `self = this`: a variable that holds `this`. Destructuring `this` (`const { x } = this`) is not reported.

upstream.note: the options (`allowDestructuring`, `allowedNames`) keep their defaults

rules.why:
The alias is a leftover of code that needed `this` inside a function that has its own `this`. An arrow function takes the `this` of the surrounding code without it, and the alias lets a reader take `self` for something other than `this`.

To fix, use an arrow function, or `bind`.

rules.description: Reports a line that begins with `(`, `[` or a template literal right after a line that ends an expression, where the two lines are one expression: `var d = a` followed by `(b);` calls `a(b)`. A line that begins with `/`, `+` or another operator is not reported.

example.input:
const a = b
  (c || d).e();

rules.why:
Automatic semicolon insertion does not insert a semicolon before `(`, `[` or a template, so the new line continues the expression above: `a` followed by `(b)` is a call and followed by `[b]` is a property access, and the program runs with a different meaning than the layout shows.

To fix, end the statement with a semicolon, or join the lines on purpose.

rules.description: Reports a type parameter constrained to `any` or `unknown` (`<T extends unknown>`, also with a default).
rules.why:
Every type parameter already accepts any type, so `extends unknown` and `extends any` restrict nothing and add noise (`extends any` also lets a reader think the check is turned off by choice).

To fix, remove the constraint.

rules.description: Reports a conditional expression whose two arms are both boolean literals: `a ? true : false` (the same as `!!a`), `a ? false : true` (`!a`), and `a ? true : true`. A conditional with one non-boolean arm is not reported.

upstream.note: the `defaultAssignment` option is not supported

rules.why:
The condition is already the boolean value, or its negation, so the conditional only restates it in a longer form.

To fix, write the condition (or `!` of it); use `Boolean(a)` where a real boolean is needed from a value that is not one.

rules.description: Reports `return`, `throw`, and a `break` or `continue` that leaves the `finally` block, written in a `finally`. A `break` or `continue` of a loop inside the block, and a `return` in a function declared in the block, are not reported.
rules.why:
A jump out of `finally` replaces how the `try` ended: a `return` there discards the value returned by the `try` and swallows an exception that was being thrown, so errors disappear without a trace.

To fix, move the jump out of `finally` (after the `try` statement), or handle the error in a `catch`.

rules.description: Reports the global type `Function` used as a type, as an `interface ... extends` target and as an `implements` target. A class that `extends Function` (a value) is not reported.
rules.why:
`Function` accepts any callable value, and calling one takes any arguments and returns `any`, so the compiler no longer checks the call.

To fix, write the signature (`(x: number) => string`), or `(...args: never[]) => unknown` for any function without losing the check.

rules.description: Reports `!a in b` and `!a instanceof B`, where the `!` is written without parentheses on the left operand. `!(a in b)` and `(!a) in b` are not reported.

upstream.note: the `enforceForOrderingRelations` option is not supported

rules.why:
The `!` binds tighter than `in` and `instanceof`, so `!a in b` tests whether the key `false` (the negation of `a`) is in `b`, and `!a instanceof B` is always `false` for a boolean. The test the author meant, the negation of the whole expression, is never made.

To fix, write `!(a in b)` or `!(a instanceof B)`.

rules.description: Reports a `catch` clause whose only statement is `throw` of the caught error, as in `catch (e) { throw e; }`. It is also reported when the `try` has a `finally`. A `catch` that does more, or that throws something else, is not reported.
rules.why:
A catch that only rethrows has the same effect as no catch: the error goes on up with its stack, so the clause is noise that makes a reader look for handling that is not there.

To fix, delete the `catch` (keep the `finally`, if there is one) or handle the error there.

rules.description: Reports a backslash before a character that needs no escape, in a string (`'\d'`), a template literal or a regex literal (`/\-/`, `/\_/`). Valid escapes (`\n`, `\t`, `\\`, `\'`, `\"`, `\x41`, `\u0041`, `\0`, a line continuation) are not reported, and neither are a `\-` in the middle of a character class (`/[a\-z]/`), `\^` at the start of one and `\/` in a regex literal.

upstream.note: regex `v` flag classes are read like `u` classes
`\/` counts as useless, as the plugin reports it

rules.why:
In a string the backslash before such a character is dropped: `'\d'` is just `d`, not the digit class the author may have meant for a regex, and in a regex a useless escape hides which characters are special. The intended meaning is lost whichever way it was read.

To fix, remove the backslash, or double it to get a real backslash (`'\\d'`).

rules.description: Reports an expression statement whose value is thrown away and that has no effect of its own: a name, a literal, a member access or an operator expression (`x + y;`, `x.y;`, `-x;`, `x ? y : z;`). Calls, assignments, `delete` and `void` are not reported; a directive such as `"use strict"` is, as it is a string. What counts as pure is the `#pure` tag of the language's grammar: Python's table has names, literals, member accesses and list, set and dict displays, so `x + 1`, `x == 2` and `-x` are not reported there. Off by default.

upstream.note: the options keep their defaults
the options keep their defaults

rules.why:
The statement is evaluated and dropped, so it does nothing. It is typically a line that was meant to be a call (a missing `()`), a comparison written where an assignment was meant, or what is left of a deleted line.

To fix, delete it, or write the call or the assignment it was meant to be.

rules.description: Reports a `var` declaration (also `declare var` in TypeScript). `let` and `const` are not reported.
rules.why:
A `var` belongs to the whole function, not to the block, and is hoisted: it can be read before its line (as `undefined`) and declared twice in one scope without an error. `let` and `const` are limited to their block, a second declaration is an error, and `const` states that the binding does not change.

To fix, use `const` where the variable is not assigned again, otherwise `let`.

rules.description: Reports a `with` statement.
rules.why:
Inside `with (obj) { ... }` every name may be a property of `obj` or a variable, and which one it is depends on `obj` at run time, so neither a reader nor a tool can tell what `b` in `with (a) { b }` refers to. The statement is a syntax error in strict mode and in ES modules, so a file that uses it cannot be turned into a module later.

To fix, name the object in each access (`a.b`) or copy the properties you need into variables before the block.

rules.description: Reports the global types `BigInt`, `Boolean`, `Number`, `Object`, `String` and `Symbol` used as type names. The lower-case primitives are not reported.
rules.why:
`String` and the like are the types of the wrapper objects (`new String('a')`), not of the primitive values, and a primitive is assignable to them only by accident of the language. `Object` accepts every value except `null` and `undefined`, numbers and strings included.

To fix, write `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `bigint` or `symbol`; for any non-primitive value write `object`.

rules.description: Reports a literal type that only repeats the literal it is given: `let a: 'a' = 'a'`, `'a' as 'a'` and `<'a'>'a'`. A type that differs from the value (`let a: 'a' = 'b'` is a type error, not reported) and `as const` are not reported.

example.input:

class C { p: "a" = "a"; q = 1 as 1; r = <"a">"a"; s = "a" as "b"; }

rules.why:
The literal is written twice and the two copies can drift apart when one is edited. `as const` says it once and keeps the literal type.

To fix, write `let a = 'a' as const`.

rules.description: Reports a `let` variable that is assigned once and could be a `const`: the single write is its initializer, a `for-in` or `for-of` head, or the first assignment statement in the same block as the declaration. A variable written in a nested block or function, a `let` of a `for (;;)` head, and a destructuring that assigns members or outer names are not reported.

upstream.note: the options keep their defaults (`destructuring: any`, `ignoreReadBeforeAssign: false`)

rules.why:
A `let` says the variable changes. When it never does, the keyword misleads the reader into looking for the later assignment, and `const` lets the compiler stop one.

To fix, write `const`.

rules.description: Reports `arguments` used in an ordinary function, except as the object of a member read by name (`arguments.length`). `arguments[0]` and passing `arguments` on are reported; an arrow function has no `arguments` of its own and is not checked.
rules.why:
`arguments` is an array-like object, not an array, and is tied to the function in ways that disable some optimizations, so `arguments.map(...)` fails. A rest parameter (`...args`) is a real array and shows in the parameter list.

To fix, declare `...args`.

rules.description: Reports `f.apply(undefined, args)`, `f.apply(null, args)`, `o.m.apply(o, args)` and `o['m'].apply(o, args)`, where the first argument is `null`, `undefined`, or the same object that the method is read from. `f.apply(this, args)`, `o.m.apply(p, args)` with another object, and an array literal or a spread (`...args`) as the arguments are not reported.
rules.why:
When the call keeps the same `this`, `apply` only spreads an array into arguments, which the spread syntax says directly: `f(...args)` and `o.m(...args)`. The `apply` form needs the reader to know the first argument is ignored.

To fix, write the call with `...args`.

rules.description: A name declared again in the same scope (`var` twice, a `var` and a parameter, two functions). In TypeScript files declaration merging (interfaces, namespaces, a class with an interface) is allowed. Built-in globals are not checked.

rules.description: Reports a generator (`function*`, a generator method, `async function*`) that has statements but no `yield`. An empty generator is not reported.
rules.why:
A generator that never yields produces no values: iterating it runs the body once and ends at once. That is the mistake of a `function*` that was meant to be a normal function, or of a `yield` that was left out.

To fix, add the `yield`, or drop the `*`.

rules.description: Reports a comparison with `NaN` (`NaN` or `Number.NaN` on either side of `==`, `!=`, `===`, `!==`, `<`, `>`...), and `NaN` as the `switch` discriminant or as a `case` test. `isNaN(a)` and `Number.isNaN(a)` are not reported.

A field whose name begins with an underscore (StyleCop SA1309); the option `fields` is the expression a field name must match.

options.description: Regular expression the name of a field must match; empty: not checked.
options.name: fields

rules.description: The file name, up to its first dot and ignoring case, is the name of the first type in the file; a generic type may also be written `Name{T,U}`. Not checked when that type is partial. No fix.

example.input: class Orders { }

rules.description: `<inheritdoc />` without `cref` on a type without a base list, or on a member that neither overrides nor implements anything (a constructor whose signature matches a base constructor is fine). No fix.

Members are out of order. Compared with the member before, in the order of the `element_order` option: the kind (fields, constructors, finalizers, delegates, events, enums, interfaces, properties, indexers, operators, methods, structs, classes; in a namespace or file: namespaces, delegates, enums, interfaces, structs, classes), the access (public, internal, protected internal, protected, private protected, private), constants before other fields, static before instance members, readonly fields before the others. A trait only counts between members that agree on the traits listed before it. No fix: moving members would have to take their comments and directives along.

options.description: The traits that decide the order, most important first. A trait that is left out is not checked.
options.name: element_order

rules.description: A type, member, field or enum item that StyleCop's defaults ask to document (public, protected or internal, in types that are too; members of an interface, explicit interface implementations and enum items are public; partial declarations are left out) has no `///` comment before it. Private members are left alone. No fix.

upstream.note: Only methods and constructors, no minimum line count.
Only types, no scope option.
No stuttering check (a name that starts with the package name), no own-declaration check for `var a, B`; a method that is sortable through methods in another file of the package is reported

rules.description: A comment between the head of an `if`, `else`, `while`, `do`, `for`, `foreach`, `lock`, `try`, `catch`, `finally`, `switch`, `checked` or `unchecked` and its `{`. Put it inside the block or above the statement.
A control character (below U+0020) in the constant string given to `new Regex(...)` and the static methods of `Regex`, written raw or as an escape.
A `<summary>` that starts with the text Visual Studio generates, "Summary description for ...". Skipped when the comment has `<inheritdoc />`. No fix.

`new S()` of a value type with an implicit parameterless constructor and no initializer: write `default(S)` (`Guid.Empty`, `CancellationToken.None`, `IntPtr.Zero`, the enum member with value 0 where they exist). No fix for a target-typed `new()`.
A `<placeholder>` element in a documentation comment. No fix.

A `///` comment that holds only text, no XML element: a plain comment written with documentation slashes. The fix writes `//`, unless the comment documents a declaration (it would remove documentation).
Two elements of one documentation comment with the same text (a copied and pasted `<param>`, for example). Empty elements and "The parameter is not used." are ignored. No fix.
An attribute with empty parentheses: `[Foo()]` is `[Foo]`. Parentheses with a comment in them are left alone.

An anonymous method with an empty parameter list: `delegate() { }` is `delegate { }`. Parentheses with a comment in them are left alone. The fix is unsafe: without a parameter list the method also converts to delegate types that have parameters, which can change which overload is chosen.

A lone `;` is a statement that does nothing. A statement labelled `label: ;` is allowed. The fix removes the statement (its whole line when it is alone on it), or turns an empty loop or `if` body into `{ }`; it is not offered for the only statement of a switch section. Overlaps compiler CS0642 for `if (x);`.
A character class in the constant string given to `new Regex(...)` and the static methods of `Regex`, in which a combining mark follows another character.

upstream.note: the surrogate pair, emoji modifier, flag and joined-sequence checks are not made

rules.description: Two or more spaces outside a character class in the string given to `new Regex(...)` and the static methods of `Regex`.
A `#region` inside a block (a method, accessor or lambda body, or any block in one); regions belong between members. No fix.

`#region` hides code behind a label. Reported on every `#region` outside a block (a region inside a block is `no-region-in-body`'s), in disabled `#if` branches too; no fix, because removing a pair is a judgment call.
A `<returns>` on a method or delegate that returns `void`. The fix removes the element with its line when it is alone on it.
`base.M()` or `base[i]` where the type does not override the member, so `this` binds to the same one. The fix writes `this`.
Reports an import of every name of a package or module (`import a.b.*;` in Java and Kotlin, `from a import *` in Python, `import . "fmt"` in Go). A named import is not reported. Off by default.

example.input:
package a

import (
	. "fmt"
	"os"
	_ "embed"
	m "math"
)

import . "strings"

options.description: The aliases that bring in every name of the imported package
options.name: wildcard_aliases

upstream.note: No allow-list option.

rules.why:
A wildcard hides where a name comes from, and a name added to the package later can silently clash with one in the file or change which one a call reaches. Tools and readers cannot tell from the imports what the file uses.

To fix, import the names the file uses.

rules.description: `int?` instead of `Nullable<int>` or `System.Nullable<int>`. Name-based: a type of your own called `Nullable` is reported too. Not reported in `using` aliases, `nameof`, `typeof(Nullable<>)` and before a member access (`Nullable<int>.Equals`).

A member or element access on an expression the compiler's nullable analysis says may be null. Only code under `#nullable enable` is checked. Off by default: the compiler reports the same thing as CS8602.

A property summary starts with "Gets", "Sets" or "Gets or sets" ("Gets a value indicating whether" and so on for `bool`), as the property's accessors reachable from outside the type say. The type is read from the declaration (`bool`, `Boolean`, `System.Boolean`). The fix replaces the start of the text and lower-cases what follows.

upstream.note: a property whose type is an alias of `System.Boolean` (using alias) is not recognized as `bool`

rules.description: A property summary says "Gets or sets" while one of the accessors is not reachable from outside the type (`private set`, `internal get` on a public property). The fix replaces the start of the text with the one that matches the visible accessor.
A field, property, method or event of the containing type used by its simple name. The fix writes `this.` before it.
A `using` directive inside a namespace whose name is not written fully qualified (it resolves relative to the enclosing namespace). The fix writes the full name, unless it has type arguments.

A `using` directive that nothing in the file needs (the compiler's hidden CS8019, IDE0005 in the SDK analyzers). Not reported in a file that has compiler errors or `#if` regions, because unresolved or inactive code could be the one using it.
One attribute per attribute list: `[A, B]` becomes `[A]` and `[B]`. Lists on parameters and type parameters are left alone. The fix is not offered when the list has a comment in it.

One field or event per declaration: `int a, b;` becomes `int a;` and `int b;`, each with the attributes, modifiers and type of the original. The fix is not offered when the declaration has a comment in it.
A file holds one class or record: every later one is reported, more parts of the first class (when it is partial) excepted. Structs, interfaces, enums and delegates are not counted. No fix.
A file declares one namespace: every later one, nested ones included, is reported. No fix.
`SuppressMessage` needs a `Justification` that says something: not missing, `null`, empty, blank or `"<Pending>"`. Matches the attribute by name. No fix.

A tuple type in the signature of a method, constructor, property, indexer, conversion operator or delegate whose elements have no names. Overrides and implementations of interface members are left alone (their names are not the member's to choose). No fix.

A value is stored in a local variable and no path reads it before it is overwritten or the variable goes out of scope (a dead store). Variables that are captured or whose address is taken are not checked; a variable that is never read at all is reported by `unused-variable` instead. Overlaps the SDK analyzer IDE0059 (unnecessary assignment).

example.input: class A { int F() { int n = 0; n = G(); return n; } int H() { int m = 0; m = 1; m = G(); return m; } int G() => 1; }

rules.description: A private field, method, property or event that no file of the project uses (`analysis: deep`). Members with attributes, overrides, interface implementations, `extern` and `partial` methods are left alone, and so are the private                   methods named in `reflection_methods` of a type derived from one of                   `reflection_base_types` (a framework calls them by reflection; the `csharp/unity`                   preset lists Unity's). Overlaps the SDK analyzers IDE0051 (unused private member) and IDE0052 (unread private member).

options.description: Names of base classes whose derived types are called by a framework                           through reflection (with `reflection_methods`). A base is matched by its                           simple name anywhere up the inheritance chain, also when the project                           does not load its assembly.
options.name: reflection_base_types

options.description: Names of private methods that count as used in a type derived from                           one of `reflection_base_types`.
options.name: reflection_methods

rules.description: A local variable or catch variable that is never used (the compiler's CS0168), or is only assigned constants and never read (CS0219). Variables captured by lambdas or local functions count as used. Off by default: the compiler already warns (CS0168, CS0219).

example.input:
function F {
    $unused = 1
    $read = 2
    "$read"
    $member = @{}
    $member.x = 1
    $list = @(1)
    $list[0] = 2
    $a, $b = 1, 2
    $script:s = 1
    $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
    $count = 1
    $count++
    $block = 1
    $f = { $block }
    & $f
    $Mixed = 1
    "$mixed"
    ${with space} = 1
    ${with space}
    $q = 1
    $script:t = $q
    $splat = @{}
    Get-Item @splat
    $u = 1
}

upstream.note: the options keep their defaults; `/*exported*/` and `/*global*/` comments are not read; a JSX tag counts as a use

The shared scope model, where a name is looked up through the blocks around it, so a read in an inner block of a name the inner block assigns itself counts for the outer one; the module counts by name inside each block. A scope that reads `$PSBoundParameters` is not checked (a documented difference).
A name the whole file assigns and never reads; the file is one scope, `local` is not told apart.
the options keep their defaults; `.d.ts` files and `declare module` blocks are not treated as used

rules.description: A lambda instead of an anonymous method. The fix is offered when the anonymous method has a parameter list and no comment before its body; `delegate { }` without one converts to delegate types with any parameters, so it has no fix.

A numeric literal cast to `long`, `ulong`, `uint`, `float`, `double` or `decimal` when the literal's own type differs: `(long)1` is `1L`. Not reported for hexadecimal and binary literals cast to a floating-point type, which have no suffix.
`string.Empty` instead of `""` (or `@""`). Not reported where a constant is required: `const`, attribute arguments, default parameter values, `case` labels and patterns.

upstream.note: Only the `string.Empty` direction; no option for the opposite style (RCS1078) because no preset needs it

rules.description: `ValueTuple<int, int>` and `ValueTuple.Create(a, b)` where tuple syntax `(int, int)` and `(a, b)` is available (not inside an expression tree). The fix is offered for types and `ValueTuple.Create` calls.

`using` directives of a file or namespace are out of order: System first (`system_first`), names in alphabetical order (`compare`), and with the options `static_position` and `alias_position` set to `after`, `using static` directives after the plain ones and aliases after those, each group sorted. `global using` and `using unsafe` stay where they are, and a list restarts at a directive that has a preprocessor directive in front of it (the fix leaves such lists alone). Comments on lines of their own stay where they are; a comment after a directive moves with it. Overlaps the SDK analyzers' `dotnet_sort_system_directives_first` .editorconfig key.

options.description: Put `System` and `System.*` before the other namespaces.
options.name: system_first

options.description: `ordinal` compares code points; `culture` ignores case (and puts punctuation before digits before letters, a lower-case name before an upper-case one that is otherwise equal); `culture_ignore_case` leaves names that differ only in case in their order.
options.name: compare

options.description: `after`: `using static` directives come after the plain usings, sorted (System ones first with `system_first`); `keep`: they stay where they are.
options.name: static_position

options.description: `after`: alias directives come after all other usings, sorted by alias name; `keep`: they stay where they are.
options.name: alias_position

upstream.note: no blank-line group handling
no blank-line group handling
no blank-line group handling

rules.description: A `using` directive outside the namespace declaration in a file that has one (StyleCop SA1200). No fix: moving a directive changes how names are looked up.
